text: Socrates (470–399 BCE) wrote nothing himself; everything we know about his philosophy comes from the dialogues of his student Plato and the writings of Xenophon.

Plato's Allegory of the Cave, found in 'The Republic,' depicts prisoners chained in a cave who mistake shadows on a wall for reality, illustrating his distinction between the world of appearances and the world of true Forms.
Aristotle, Plato's student, rejected the Theory of Forms and argued that universal concepts exist within individual things (immanent realism) rather than in a separate transcendent realm.

The Socratic Method is a form of cooperative argumentative dialogue in which questions are asked to expose contradictions in a person's beliefs, leading them toward greater self-knowledge and clarity of thought.

Descartes' famous statement 'Cogito, ergo sum' ('I think, therefore I am') in his 1637 'Discourse on the Method' is considered the foundational proposition of Western modern philosophy, establishing the existence of the self through doubt.

Immanuel Kant's 'Critique of Pure Reason' (1781) proposed that space, time, and causality are not features of an objective reality but categories imposed by the human mind on experience — a 'Copernican revolution' in philosophy.

Kant's Categorical Imperative states: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law' — a deontological ethical principle based on rationality rather than consequences.

John Stuart Mill's utilitarianism holds that the morally right action is the one that produces the greatest amount of happiness (utility) for the greatest number of people — a consequentialist ethical theory.

Friedrich Nietzsche's concept of the 'Übermensch' (overman or superman) in 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' (1883) described an ideal human who creates his own values beyond conventional morality, transcending the limitations of ordinary humanity.
David Hume argued in 'A Treatise of Human Nature' (1739) that reason alone cannot motivate action; he famously wrote that 'reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.'
The Ship of Theseus paradox asks whether an object that has had all of its components replaced remains fundamentally the same object, probing questions of identity and persistence through time.

Confucius (551–479 BCE), whose teachings are recorded in 'The Analects,' emphasized virtue, loyalty, ritual propriety, and humaneness (ren) as the foundations of both personal conduct and good governance.

Laozi (Lao Tzu), the founder of Taoism, taught that the Tao (Way) is the underlying principle of the universe; his text, the 'Tao Te Ching,' advocates for wu wei (non-action), simplicity, and harmony with nature.

The trolley problem, introduced by Philippa Foot in 1967 and popularized by Judith Jarvis Thomson, is an ethical thought experiment asking whether it is morally permissible to actively cause one death to prevent five.

Plato's 'Meno' explores whether virtue can be taught; the dialogue includes the paradox of inquiry: one cannot search for what one knows (already having it) or for what one does not know (not recognizing it when found).

Zhuangzi (4th century BCE) is associated with Taoism's more mystical strand; his butterfly dream — did he dream he was a butterfly, or is a butterfly now dreaming of being him? — explores the nature of reality and identity.

Aristotle identified four causes to explain things: material (what it is made of), formal (what shape or form it has), efficient (what made it), and final (what it is for) — the last being the teleological purpose.

Epicurus (341–270 BCE) taught that the highest good is pleasure (hedone), particularly ataraxia (tranquility) and aponia (freedom from physical pain), achieved through simple living, friendship, and philosophical reflection.

The Stoics, founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE, taught that virtue is the only true good and that one must accept what is outside one's control with equanimity; their ideas influenced Roman philosophers Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius.

Baruch Spinoza argued in his 'Ethics' (1677) that God and Nature are one and the same infinite substance (pantheism), and that free will is an illusion arising from ignorance of the causes that determine our actions.

John Locke argued in his 'Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) that the mind at birth is a 'tabula rasa' (blank slate) and all knowledge comes from sensory experience — the foundation of empiricist epistemology.

George Berkeley (1685–1753) argued that matter does not exist independently of perception; his famous thesis esse est percipi ('to be is to be perceived') asserts that objects exist only when perceived by a mind.

G.W.F. Hegel's dialectical method describes historical progress as a conflict between a thesis and an antithesis, resolving in a synthesis that then becomes a new thesis — a process he called Aufhebung (sublation).
Karl Marx adapted Hegel's dialectic and applied it to material conditions (dialectical materialism), arguing that historical change is driven by class conflict and economic forces rather than ideas.

Jean-Paul Sartre's existentialism, summed up as 'existence precedes essence,' holds that humans first exist and then create their own meaning, nature, and purpose — there is no pre-given human essence.
Simone de Beauvoir's 'The Second Sex' (1949) argued that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,' situating gender as a social and historical construction rather than a biological given.

Albert Camus introduced the concept of 'the Absurd' — the conflict between the human tendency to seek meaning and the universe's silence — in 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942), arguing one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz famously argued in 'Theodicy' (1710) that our world is 'the best of all possible worlds,' as a perfectly good God would have chosen it; this view was satirized by Voltaire in 'Candide.'

The philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198) was instrumental in translating and commenting on Aristotle's works, preserving and transmitting Greek philosophy to medieval Europe through Arabic scholarship.

Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037), the Islamic physician-philosopher, developed the 'floating man' thought experiment — a person suspended in air with no sensory input would still be aware of his own existence — anticipating Descartes' cogito.

Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), in his 'Incoherence of the Philosophers,' attacked the Islamic neo-Aristotelian philosophers (including Avicenna), arguing that their claims about the eternity of the world contradicted Islamic theology.

The Indian philosopher Nagarjuna (c. 150–250 CE) founded the Madhyamaka school of Buddhist philosophy, arguing that all phenomena are empty (shunyata) of inherent existence and exist only through dependent origination.

Adi Shankaracharya (8th century CE) articulated Advaita Vedanta, the non-dualist school of Hindu philosophy, which holds that Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (the individual self) are one and the same.

The Nyaya school of Indian philosophy, founded around the 2nd century BCE, developed detailed logic and epistemology and is particularly known for its theory of inference (anumana) and its arguments for the existence of God.

The pre-Socratic philosopher Heraclitus (c. 535–475 BCE) held that everything is in constant flux ('you can never step in the same river twice') and that the underlying unity of opposites is the Logos (reason or word).

Parmenides (c. 515–450 BCE) argued that reality is a single, unchanging, indivisible whole, and that change and multiplicity are illusions of the senses — a position at odds with Heraclitus's flux doctrine.
Zeno of Elea (c. 490–430 BCE) devised famous paradoxes — including Achilles and the Tortoise and the Arrow paradox — to defend Parmenides' view that motion and change are illusory.

Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE) held that numbers are the ultimate reality and the fundamental principle underlying the structure of the cosmos — a view that influenced mathematics, music theory, and philosophy.

The Cynics, led by Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BCE), rejected conventional social values, wealth, and power; Diogenes reportedly lived in a barrel and told Alexander the Great to step out of his sunlight.
John Rawls' 'A Theory of Justice' (1971) proposed the 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment: principles of justice should be chosen by rational people who do not know their own place in society.
Robert Nozick's 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974) responded to Rawls by defending libertarianism, arguing that a minimal state is justified but any more extensive state violates individual rights.

Ludwig Wittgenstein's early work in the 'Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus' (1921) held that the limits of language are the limits of one's world; his later 'Philosophical Investigations' (1953) reversed many of those views.

Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead's 'Principia Mathematica' (1910–1913) attempted to derive all mathematical truths from logical axioms alone, a project undermined by Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems in 1931.

The problem of evil asks how an all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good God can be compatible with the existence of evil and suffering; it has challenged theologians and philosophers from Epicurus through Leibniz to the present day.

Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855), often called the father of existentialism, identified three stages of human existence: the aesthetic (pleasure-seeking), the ethical (duty-bound), and the religious (faith-based).

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) argued in 'The World as Will and Representation' that the fundamental nature of reality is a blind, irrational, striving force (Will), and that suffering is the default state of existence.

The mind-body problem asks how the immaterial mind (consciousness, thoughts) can interact with the physical brain and body; Descartes proposed dualism (two separate substances), while later thinkers proposed physicalism or functionalism.
Thomas Nagel's 1974 paper 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' argued that subjective conscious experience (qualia) cannot be fully explained by objective physical or functional descriptions alone.

Mary's Room, Frank Jackson's 1982 thought experiment, features a color scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows all physical facts about color but learns something new upon seeing red — an argument against physicalism.

Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832), founder of utilitarianism, invented the 'felicific calculus' to quantify pleasure and pain, and his preserved body (the 'Auto-Icon') is displayed at University College London.
Plato's 'Republic' envisions a philosopher-king as the ideal ruler — someone who has attained true knowledge of the Good and can therefore govern justly, uncorrupted by self-interest.

Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' defines happiness (eudaimonia) not as pleasure but as the active exercise of virtue in accordance with reason — a flourishing or thriving life, not merely a pleasant one.

Thomas Hobbes argued in 'Leviathan' (1651) that without a strong central authority, human life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — justifying absolute sovereignty as a necessary social contract.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued in 'The Social Contract' (1762) that sovereignty resides in the 'general will' of the people, and famously wrote 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'

The Socratic problem of the 'good life' remains central in ethics: is it pleasure (Epicurus), virtue (Aristotle and Stoics), duty (Kant), or the fulfillment of desire (Hume)? Different schools give fundamentally different answers.

Martin Heidegger's 'Being and Time' (1927) introduced Dasein (being-in-the-world) and argued that authentic existence requires confronting one's own mortality and owning one's existence rather than conforming to 'the they' (das Man).

Phenomenology, founded by Edmund Husserl (1859–1938), studies the structure of experience and consciousness from the first-person perspective, bracketing assumptions about external reality to focus on how objects appear to consciousness.

Michel Foucault's 'Discipline and Punish' (1975) analyzed how modern prisons, schools, and hospitals use surveillance and normalization as forms of social control — introducing the concept of the 'panopticon' as a metaphor for power.
Pragmatism, the distinctly American philosophy developed by Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, holds that the truth of an idea is determined by its practical consequences.

The philosopher Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972) argued that failing to prevent easily preventable suffering is morally equivalent to causing it, calling on wealthy individuals to donate substantially to aid.

Derek Parfit's 'Reasons and Persons' (1984) explored personal identity, arguing that the self is not a separately existing entity and that common sense moral intuitions about identity are philosophically untenable.

Kwame Anthony Appiah's 'Cosmopolitanism' (2006) argues for a philosophical commitment to a world in which people are citizens of the world first, while still cherishing particular cultural identities.

Niccolò Machiavelli's 'The Prince' (1513) broke from the idealism of classical political philosophy, advising rulers to act effectively rather than virtuously, and arguing that it is better to be feared than loved if one cannot be both.

The Gettier problem (1963), described in Edmund Gettier's three-page paper, demolished the classic definition of knowledge as 'justified true belief' by presenting cases where a justified true belief is not genuine knowledge.

The philosopher Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) proposed the ontological argument for God's existence: God is defined as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' and if God existed only in the mind, a greater being could be imagined.

Thomas Aquinas's 'Five Ways' (Quinque Viae) in 'Summa Theologica' offered five arguments for God's existence, including the cosmological argument from motion, causation, contingency, degree of perfection, and design.

The philosophical zombie (p-zombie) thought experiment, associated with David Chalmers, imagines a being physically identical to a human but lacking any conscious experience — used to argue that consciousness cannot be reduced to physical processes.

Plato's Theory of Recollection holds that learning is actually remembering knowledge the soul possessed before birth; this was used in 'Meno' to explain how an uneducated slave boy could understand geometric truths.

The Bhagavad Gita, part of the Mahabharata epic (c. 500 BCE–200 CE), presents a philosophical dialogue between Prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, covering dharma, karma, yoga, and the nature of the self.

Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha (c. 563–483 BCE), taught that suffering (dukkha) arises from craving and ignorance, and can be overcome through the Noble Eightfold Path — forming the core of Buddhist philosophy.

Gottlob Frege (1848–1925), often considered the father of analytic philosophy, distinguished between the 'sense' (Sinn) and the 'reference' (Bedeutung) of expressions — 'the morning star' and 'the evening star' have the same reference but different senses.

Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' (1990) argued that gender is performative — it is constituted by repeated acts and expressions rather than expressing an inner essence — influencing feminist and queer theory.

The philosophy of language's 'linguistic turn,' prominent in the 20th century, held that many philosophical problems are fundamentally about language and can be clarified or dissolved by careful analysis of how words are used.

Hannah Arendt's 'The Origins of Totalitarianism' (1951) and 'The Human Condition' (1958) explored the nature of political action, the 'banality of evil' (observing Eichmann), and the distinction between the public and private realm.

Plato divided the soul into three parts: the rational (logistikon), the spirited (thymoeides), and the appetitive (epithymetikon), corresponding to the three classes of his ideal state — philosopher-kings, warriors, and producers.

The Analytic-Continental divide is a major split in Western philosophy: analytic philosophy (dominant in the English-speaking world) emphasizes clarity and logical rigor, while Continental philosophy (from mainland Europe) focuses on broader cultural and historical questions.

The philosopher Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) is considered a founder of sociology, historiography, and economics; in the 'Muqaddimah' he developed a cyclical theory of history driven by social cohesion (asabiyyah).

Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE), founder of the Mohist school of Chinese philosophy, advocated impartial concern for all people regardless of kinship (jian ai), in contrast to Confucius's graded love based on familial relationships.

The Jain philosophical concept of anekantavada ('many-sidedness') holds that truth and reality are complex and can be viewed from many perspectives, none of which is complete on its own — a sophisticated theory of epistemic pluralism.

Immanuel Kant drew a distinction between analytic propositions (true by definition, e.g., 'all bachelors are unmarried') and synthetic propositions (true by fact, e.g., 'it is raining'), and controversially posited 'synthetic a priori' truths.

The philosophical school of Skepticism, originating with Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BCE), held that knowledge is impossible and that the wise response is epoché — suspension of judgment — leading to tranquility (ataraxia).

W.V.O. Quine's essay 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) attacked the distinction between analytic and synthetic truths and the theory of meaning, arguing that our statements face experience as a corporate body rather than individually.

Karl Popper's philosophy of science introduced the criterion of falsifiability: a theory is scientific only if it makes predictions that could in principle be shown to be false by experiment — distinguishing science from pseudoscience.

Thomas Kuhn's 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962) introduced the concept of 'paradigm shifts' — arguing that science progresses not by gradual accumulation but by revolutionary changes in worldview.

Virtue ethics, associated with Aristotle and revived in the 20th century by Alasdair MacIntyre and Philippa Foot, asks not 'what should I do?' but 'what kind of person should I be?' — focusing on character rather than rules or consequences.

Nishida Kitaro (1870–1945), Japan's first major original Western-style philosopher, founded the Kyoto School and developed the concept of 'pure experience' (junsui keiken) as the foundation of philosophy, influenced by William James.

The philosophical doctrine of solipsism holds that only one's own mind is certain to exist, and that external reality and other minds cannot be proven; it is an extreme consequence of Cartesian doubt.

The paradox of the heap (sorites paradox) asks: if you remove one grain from a heap of sand, is it still a heap? It exposes the vagueness of many predicates and challenges classical logic's law of excluded middle.

The Frankfurt School of critical theory, including Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, and Herbert Marcuse, combined Marxist theory with psychoanalysis to critique modern capitalism, mass culture, and the Enlightenment's dark side.

Jürgen Habermas's theory of 'communicative action' distinguishes between strategic action (aimed at success) and communicative action (aimed at mutual understanding), and grounds normative legitimacy in ideal conditions of rational discourse.

Maimonides (Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, 1138–1204) in 'Guide for the Perplexed' argued that God can only be described by negative attributes (negative theology), as any positive description would limit the infinite divine nature.

The Chinese philosopher Mengzi (Mencius, c. 372–289 BCE) argued that human nature is fundamentally good and that people have innate moral sprouts (including compassion, shame, modesty, and right and wrong) that education cultivates.
Xunzi (c. 310–235 BCE) countered Mencius by arguing that human nature is inherently bad — prone to desire and conflict — and that goodness must be learned through ritual, education, and social norms.

The Upanishads (c. 800–200 BCE) are foundational texts of Indian philosophy that explore the relationship between Atman (individual self) and Brahman (universal reality), culminating in the insight 'Tat tvam asi' ('Thou art that').

Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792) argued that women's apparent inferiority was due to lack of education, not nature — making her a pioneering voice in liberal feminist philosophy.

The Euthyphro dilemma, posed in Plato's dialogue, asks: Is something good because God commands it (divine command theory), or does God command it because it is good (natural law theory)? — a perennial challenge in philosophy of religion.

Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx's 'Communist Manifesto' (1848) opens with 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' — a foundational statement of historical materialism.

The Milgram experiment (1961), while primarily psychological, raised profound philosophical questions about obedience, moral responsibility, and the conditions under which ordinary people commit atrocities.

G.E. Moore's 'open question argument' in 'Principia Ethica' (1903) held that no natural property can define 'good,' as for any natural property X, it remains an open question whether X is good — calling this error 'the naturalistic fallacy.'

The philosopher Gottfried Leibniz discovered calculus independently of Newton around the same time in the 1670s; the priority dispute between them and their supporters became one of the most notorious controversies in the history of science.

The philosopher Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) proposed that all matter is composed of tiny indivisible particles called 'atoms' (from the Greek atomos, 'uncuttable') — an ancient anticipation of modern atomic theory.
Hume's problem of induction asks why we are justified in believing that the future will resemble the past: no amount of past experience can logically guarantee that the sun will rise tomorrow.

The Chinese Legalist school (Fajia), prominent in the Warring States period, held that strict laws and punishments rather than virtue or ritual are the proper means of social order, influencing the policies of the Qin Empire.

The existentialist Albert Camus, in 'The Rebel' (1951), argued that metaphysical rebellion is the only honest response to the Absurd, and that human solidarity rather than nihilism should be its outcome.

The Liar's Paradox, attributed to Epimenides the Cretan ('All Cretans are liars'), challenges the foundations of logic: if the statement 'This sentence is false' is true, then it is false, and vice versa.

Process philosophy, developed by Alfred North Whitehead in 'Process and Reality' (1929), argues that reality is fundamentally dynamic — composed not of static substances but of events and processes of becoming.
Diogenes Laertius (3rd century CE) wrote 'Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers,' the primary ancient source for biographical information and philosophical doctrines of the Greek philosophers.

The philosopher Nelson Goodman's 'grue' paradox introduced a fictional predicate ('grue' = green before time T, blue after) to show that the problem of induction is deeper than Hume imagined — not all generalizations are equally projectible.

The Zen Buddhist koan 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' is not meant to have a logical answer; it is designed to break the discursive mind and trigger direct insight (satori) beyond conceptual reasoning.

Plato's dialogue 'Symposium' contains multiple speeches on the nature of love (eros); Socrates relays Diotima's teaching that love ultimately leads the philosopher from love of a beautiful body to love of Beauty itself.

The Analects' concept of zhengming (rectification of names) holds that social and political order depends on words accurately describing reality: if names are not correct, speech will not accord with truth.
Nietzsche's declaration 'God is dead' in 'The Gay Science' (1882) was not a literal claim about theology but a diagnosis of the collapse of the Christian moral framework in modern European culture.

Hilary Putnam's twin earth thought experiment (1973) argued that meanings are not 'in the head': if Earth and Twin Earth have identical internal states but different substances called 'water,' the meaning of 'water' still differs.

The philosophical movement of Logical Positivism (Vienna Circle, 1920s–30s), led by Moritz Schlick and Rudolf Carnap, held that meaningful statements must be either analytically true or empirically verifiable — condemning metaphysics as meaningless.

The doctrine of karma in Hindu and Buddhist philosophy holds that actions have moral consequences that shape future existences; it provides a causal framework for understanding suffering and the cycle of rebirth (samsara).

Plotinus (204–270 CE), founder of Neoplatonism, taught that all existence emanates in descending levels from a supreme principle called the One, and that the soul's purpose is to return to the One through philosophical contemplation.

The problem of free will vs. determinism asks whether human choices are truly free if every event (including brain states) is caused by prior events; compatibilists argue that free will and determinism can coexist.

Socrates' interlocutors in Plato's dialogues often begin by giving examples of virtues rather than defining virtue itself; Socrates insists on seeking the universal essence — what all virtuous acts have in common.

The ancient Skeptic Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE) codified Pyrrhonism in 'Outlines of Pyrrhonism,' arguing that for every argument on one side there is an equal argument on the other (isostheneia), so suspension of judgment is rational.

The concept of 'intersubjectivity' — the shared, social nature of consciousness and meaning — is central to phenomenology (Husserl, Merleau-Ponty) and analytic philosophy of language (Wittgenstein's private language argument).

John Dewey argued that education should not be about filling students with facts but about the development of critical thinking and problem-solving skills, making education a practice of democracy itself.

The philosopher Martha Nussbaum developed the Capabilities Approach — focusing on what people are actually able to do and be — as a more nuanced metric for human development than income-based measures.
The Sufi philosopher Ibn Arabi (1165–1240) taught the doctrine of 'Unity of Being' (Wahdat al-Wujud), arguing that all existence is a single divine being manifesting in infinite forms.
The concept of 'bad faith' (mauvaise foi) in Sartre's existentialism refers to the dishonest self-deception by which people deny their own freedom and responsibility, pretending they have no choice.

The simulation hypothesis, popularized by philosopher Nick Bostrom's 2003 paper, argues that we are likely living in a computer simulation run by a technologically advanced civilization — a modern twist on Descartes' evil demon.

The Vedanta philosopher Ramanuja (1017–1137 CE) proposed Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism), holding that Brahman is one but comprises both the supreme soul (God), individual souls, and the material world as its attributes.

The concept of 'eternal recurrence' in Nietzsche's philosophy poses a thought experiment: if you had to live your life again exactly the same way, infinitely many times, how would you live? It is a test of one's love of life.

Merleau-Ponty's 'Phenomenology of Perception' (1945) argued that embodiment is central to consciousness — the body is not an object in the world but the very means of being in the world and perceiving it.

The Prisoner's Dilemma in game theory has profound philosophical implications: rational self-interest leads to a worse outcome for all parties, suggesting the limits of purely self-interested rationality in ethics.

Alvin Plantinga developed 'reformed epistemology,' arguing that belief in God can be 'properly basic' — rationally held without evidence or argument — just as belief in other minds or the external world is accepted without proof.

The Milesian philosophers — Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes — are considered the first Western philosophers; they sought natural explanations for the cosmos, proposing water, the 'Apeiron' (the indefinite), and air as fundamental principles.

The doctrine of the 'golden mean' (mesotes) in Aristotle's ethics holds that virtue is a disposition to act in a way that is the mean between two extremes of vice — e.g., courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness.

Emmanuel Levinas argued that ethics is 'first philosophy' — preceding ontology and epistemology — and that the encounter with the Other's face is the foundational moral experience that calls us to responsibility.

Jean Baudrillard's 'Simulacra and Simulation' (1981) argued that contemporary society is dominated by simulations that have replaced reality — 'hyperreality' — where the map precedes and generates the territory.

The concept of 'reflective equilibrium,' introduced by John Rawls, is a method in ethics that achieves coherence between moral intuitions and principles by revising both until they align in a stable balance.

The early Buddhist school of Abhidharma developed a detailed analysis of reality into its ultimate constituents (dharmas) — momentary psychophysical events — in contrast to the conventional reality of everyday persons and objects.

St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) reconciled Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian theology, arguing that God is the source of all being and goodness, and that evil is not a substance but an absence or privation of good.
Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), the Subtle Doctor, introduced the concept of 'haecceity' (thisness) to explain what makes an individual thing uniquely itself — beyond its general nature or essence.
William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) formulated 'Ockham's Razor': entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity — the simplest explanation requiring the fewest assumptions is preferred.

The Midrash and Talmud contain philosophical discussions about the nature of God, ethics, and interpretation; medieval Jewish philosopher Saadia Gaon (882–942 CE) was the first to systematically reconcile Jewish theology with rationalist philosophy.

Paul Ricoeur's hermeneutics argued that interpretation of texts (and actions) requires a 'hermeneutic arc' — moving from naive understanding through structural analysis to a deeper, appropriated understanding that changes the interpreter.

The Marxist philosopher Antonio Gramsci developed the concept of 'cultural hegemony' — the idea that dominant classes maintain power not just through force but by shaping the cultural norms, values, and worldviews of the wider population.

Frantz Fanon's 'The Wretched of the Earth' (1961) applied existentialist and psychoanalytic concepts to the experience of colonial oppression, arguing that colonialism dehumanizes both colonized and colonizer.

The Nyaya school's theory of perception (pratyaksha) distinguishes between indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) — bare sensation without conceptual content — and determinate perception (savikalpaka) — classified and conceptualized awareness.

Blaise Pascal's Wager argues that a rational person should believe in God because if God exists and you believe, you gain infinite happiness; if God does not exist and you believe, you lose little — making belief the rational bet.

The Daoist concept of 'wu wei' (non-action or effortless action) does not mean doing nothing, but rather acting in harmony with the natural flow of things rather than forcing outcomes through deliberate exertion.

Jacques Derrida's deconstruction methodology aimed to expose the unstable hierarchies and contradictions within texts, arguing that meaning is never fully present but always deferred through chains of differences (différance).

John Austin's speech act theory (1955) distinguished between locutionary acts (the literal meaning of words), illocutionary acts (what is accomplished in speaking, e.g., promising, ordering), and perlocutionary acts (the effects produced).

The concept of 'moral luck' (Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, 1976) holds that morality is influenced by factors outside our control, challenging Kant's view that moral worth depends solely on good will.

Richard Rorty's neo-pragmatism in 'Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature' (1979) rejected the idea that the mind mirrors reality, arguing that philosophy should abandon its quest for foundations and serve as a cultural conversation.

The Vaisheshika school of Indian philosophy, founded by Kanada (c. 6th century BCE), proposed an atomistic theory of matter, categorizing all of reality into substance, quality, motion, universal, particular, and inherence.

The thought experiment of Theseus's paradox extends to personal identity: if all neurons and cells in a person's body are replaced over time, is it the same person? This is the basis of psychological continuity theories of identity.

The Chinese philosopher Wang Yangming (1472–1529) championed the unity of knowledge and action (zhizhng heyi), arguing that to truly know the good is to act upon it — knowledge and action cannot be genuinely separated.

The philosophical doctrine of 'occasionalism,' developed by Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), holds that God is the only true cause; apparent causal relations between events are merely 'occasions' for divine intervention.

Epictetus (c. 50–135 CE), born into slavery, became one of the most influential Stoic philosophers; his 'Enchiridion' begins with the core Stoic insight: 'Some things are in our control and others not.'

The 'bundle theory' of personal identity, proposed by Hume, holds that the self is not a unified, persistent entity but merely a 'bundle or collection of different perceptions which succeed each other with inconceivable rapidity.'

Marcus Aurelius (121–180 CE), Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher, wrote 'Meditations' as a personal journal of philosophical reflections — emphasizing duty, reason, and the transience of all earthly things.

The Mimamsa school of Indian philosophy, focused on interpreting Vedic ritual texts, developed detailed theories of language and meaning, holding that words and their meanings are eternal and uncreated.

The philosopher Charles Taylor's 'Sources of the Self' (1989) argued that modern identity is constituted by 'moral frameworks' — orientations toward what is good and meaningful — and that disengaged views of the self are philosophically incoherent.

The concept of 'alienation' in Marxist philosophy describes the estrangement of workers from their labor, from the products they create, from other people, and from their own human nature under capitalist production.

The Emotivist theory in metaethics, associated with A.J. Ayer (1936) and Charles Stevenson, holds that moral statements do not express propositions but rather express emotions or attitudes — they are neither true nor false.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt's concept of 'natality' holds that the capacity to begin something new — to take initiative — is the distinctive feature of human existence and the foundation of political freedom.

The Madhyamaka philosopher Chandrakirti (c. 600–650 CE) distinguished between two truths: conventional truth (the everyday world) and ultimate truth (emptiness) — arguing both are necessary for the Buddhist path.
Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–475 BCE) criticized anthropomorphic conceptions of the gods, famously observing that if horses and cows could draw, they would depict the gods as horses and cows.

The Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200 CE) developed an influential metaphysics based on the concepts of Li (principle) and Qi (material force), arguing that all things consist of these two fundamental aspects.

The philosophical movement of Transcendentalism, led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau in 19th-century America, held that the divine is immanent in nature and human nature, and that individual intuition is the highest judge of truth.

Gaston Bachelard's philosophy of science emphasized the concept of 'epistemological obstacles' — pre-scientific notions (like animism or anthropomorphism) that must be overcome for scientific knowledge to progress.

The concept of 'intersectionality,' introduced by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, describes how overlapping social identities (race, gender, class) create interconnected systems of discrimination and privilege.

Aristotle's 'Politics' argued that 'man is by nature a political animal' (zoon politikon) — humans can only fully realize their potential and live the good life within a well-ordered political community.

The brain-in-a-vat thought experiment (Hilary Putnam, 1981) asks whether you could know that you are not a disembodied brain being fed false sensory inputs by a supercomputer — raising questions about the basis of knowledge.
Elisabeth of Bohemia's correspondence with Descartes (1643) posed a sharp challenge to his mind-body dualism: how can an immaterial, unextended mind cause changes in a material, extended body?

The concept of 'ressentiment' in Nietzsche's 'On the Genealogy of Morality' (1887) described the slave morality of the weak who, unable to act, revalue their powerlessness as goodness and call the strength of the powerful evil.
Phronesis (practical wisdom) is, for Aristotle, the master virtue — the capacity to discern the right course of action in particular circumstances — and it cannot be reduced to following rules.

The Sankhya school of Indian philosophy posits that reality consists of two fundamental principles: Purusha (pure consciousness, spirit) and Prakriti (primordial matter), whose interaction gives rise to all existence.

The concept of 'interpassivity,' introduced by Robert Pfaller and Slavoj Žižek, describes a phenomenon where objects or media 'enjoy' or perform activities on our behalf — as when a laugh track laughs for us.

The Daoist classic 'Zhuangzi' includes the story of Cook Ding, who cuts an ox along natural joints with perfect skill (de), illustrating the Taoist ideal of acting in perfect accordance with the natural structure of things.

The thought experiment of 'Buridan's Ass,' attributed to 14th-century philosopher Jean Buridan, posits a donkey perfectly equidistant between two identical bales of hay that starves because it cannot rationally choose between them.

The concept of 'thick ethical concepts' (Bernard Williams) are terms like 'cruel,' 'kind,' or 'courageous' that simultaneously describe and evaluate — combining factual and normative content in a way that pure descriptive or evaluative terms cannot.

Anaxagoras (c. 510–428 BCE) proposed that Mind (Nous) is the original source of motion in the universe — the first principle that set all things in order from primordial chaos; he was prosecuted for impiety in Athens.

Antonio Damasio's 'Somatic Marker Hypothesis' in 'Descartes' Error' (1994) argued, contra Descartes, that emotions are essential to rational decision-making — patients with damage to emotion-related brain areas make disastrously poor decisions.

The doctrine of 'occasionalism' was used by Muslim theologian Al-Ash'ari (874–936 CE) and his school to argue that God continuously recreates the world moment to moment, making apparent natural laws expressions of divine habit.

The is–ought problem, or Hume's guillotine, notes that descriptive statements about what 'is' cannot on their own logically entail normative statements about what 'ought' to be — a distinction fundamental to ethics and social science.

The 'Extended Mind Thesis' by Andy Clark and David Chalmers (1998) argues that the mind is not confined to the brain and body but can incorporate external objects — like a notebook or smartphone — as genuine parts of cognition.

The philosophical problem of 'other minds' asks how we can know that other people have inner subjective experiences rather than being unconscious automata — a profound challenge for epistemology and the basis of empathy.

Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BCE) is said to have practiced his own philosophy of radical skepticism so literally that he reportedly had to be restrained from walking in front of carts, having suspended judgment about all dangers.

The philosopher Kwame Gyekye (1939–2019) developed an African communitarian philosophy balancing communal values with individual rights, arguing that African traditions offer distinct insights for political and moral philosophy.

Aristotle described 'catharsis' in the 'Poetics' as the purging or clarification of emotions like pity and fear that tragedy produces in its audience — though its precise meaning remains one of philosophy's most debated concepts.

The concept of 'ubuntu' ('I am because we are'), rooted in southern African philosophy, holds that personhood is inherently relational and communal — a person becomes fully human only through community.

The philosopher Patricia Churchland's eliminative materialism argues that folk psychological terms like 'belief,' 'desire,' and 'pain' will eventually be replaced by a mature neuroscience that more accurately describes brain states.

Max Weber's concept of 'disenchantment of the world' (Entzauberung) described the modern process by which rational, scientific thinking replaces magic, myth, and religion as the dominant framework for understanding reality.

The concept of 'supervenience' in philosophy of mind holds that mental properties supervene on physical properties — that there can be no mental difference without a physical difference — without requiring strict identity.

Aristotle's concept of 'substance' (ousia) is the fundamental category in his metaphysics — individual things like Socrates or this oak tree are primary substances, while species and genera are secondary substances.

Boethius (c. 480–524 CE), in 'The Consolation of Philosophy' (written while awaiting execution), proposed the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human free will by arguing that God's eternity is not temporal — God sees all time at once.

The Platonic dialogue 'Phaedo' describes the final hours of Socrates' life and contains his arguments for the immortality of the soul — including the cyclical argument, recollection argument, and the argument from affinity.

The philosophical school of Neo-Daoism (Xuanxue) in 3rd–4th century China reinterpreted Daoist classics in light of Confucian texts, debating the relationship between being (you) and non-being (wu) as the ultimate ground of reality.

The concept of 'negative liberty' (Isaiah Berlin, 1958) is freedom from external interference, while 'positive liberty' is the capacity or power to act autonomously — a distinction that has shaped liberal and communitarian political debates.

The Stoic philosopher Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BCE) was the third head of the Stoa and is credited with systematizing Stoic logic, physics, and ethics; ancient commentators said that without Chrysippus there would have been no Stoa.

The Wittgensteinian concept of 'language games' (Sprachspiele) in 'Philosophical Investigations' holds that meaning is use — words derive their meaning from the 'forms of life' and practices in which they are embedded.

The hard problem of consciousness, named by David Chalmers in 1995, asks why physical brain processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all — why there is 'something it is like' to be conscious.

Philosophy's seven major branches are: metaphysics (the nature of reality), epistemology (knowledge), ethics (morality), logic (reasoning), aesthetics (beauty and art), political philosophy (society and government), and philosophy of mind (consciousness and cognition).

The 'hard problem of consciousness,' coined by David Chalmers in 1995, asks why physical brain processes give rise to subjective, first-person experience (qualia) — why there is 'something it is like' to see red or feel pain, rather than all this just happening in the dark.

Functionalism in the philosophy of mind holds that mental states are defined by their functional roles — their causal relations to sensory inputs, behavioral outputs, and other mental states — rather than by their physical substrate, opening the possibility of machine consciousness.

Daniel Dennett's 'Consciousness Explained' (1991) argues against the 'Cartesian theater' view of a central observer in the mind, proposing instead that consciousness is a 'multiple drafts' process with no single location or moment where experience is 'presented.'

The Chinese Room argument by John Searle (1980) challenges the idea that a computer running the right program could understand language or have a mind: a person in a room following syntactic rules for manipulating Chinese symbols would not 'understand' Chinese even if their outputs were perfect.

Personal identity over time is debated through thought experiments like Locke's memory theory, Parfit's fission cases (teletransportation puzzles), and Williams's bodily continuity view — asking what makes a future person the same person as you today.

The Turing Test, proposed by Alan Turing in 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950), proposes that a machine should be considered intelligent if it can produce responses indistinguishable from a human's — a test still debated as both a criterion for intelligence and a philosophical thought experiment.

Gottlob Frege's distinction between Sinn (sense) and Bedeutung (reference) in 'On Sense and Reference' (1892) showed that expressions can have the same reference (the same object) but different senses — 'the morning star' and 'the evening star' both refer to Venus but convey different information.

Speech act theory, developed by J.L. Austin and elaborated by John Searle, distinguishes between locutionary acts (what is said), illocutionary acts (what is done in saying, like promising or ordering), and perlocutionary acts (the effect produced on the hearer).

W.V.O. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) challenged the analytic-synthetic distinction and the idea that each sentence in isolation faces the tribunal of experience, arguing instead for a holistic view in which beliefs form an interlocking web (the 'Duhem-Quine thesis').

Paul Grice's theory of conversational implicature (1975) explains how speakers communicate more than they literally say, guided by cooperative conversational maxims (quantity, quality, relation, manner); violations of these maxims generate implied meanings.

Saul Kripke's 'Naming and Necessity' (1980) revolutionized the philosophy of language by arguing that names are 'rigid designators' — referring to the same object in all possible worlds — and that identity statements linking natural kind terms are necessarily true though known empirically.

Karl Popper's demarcation criterion in the philosophy of science holds that a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable — capable of being proven wrong by observation — distinguishing science from metaphysics and pseudo-science.

Thomas Kuhn's 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962) introduced the concept of paradigm shifts — arguing that science progresses through periods of 'normal science' punctuated by revolutionary changes of fundamental framework when anomalies can no longer be explained.

Imre Lakatos developed the concept of 'research programmes' in the philosophy of science — a series of theories sharing a 'hard core' of assumptions surrounded by a 'protective belt' of auxiliary hypotheses — as a more sophisticated account of scientific rationality than Popper's falsificationism.

Paul Feyerabend's 'Against Method' (1975) argued that there is no single scientific method and that science advances through 'anything goes' — violating established methodological rules is sometimes necessary for progress, as Galileo demonstrated by combining astronomy with mechanics.

Edmund Husserl founded phenomenology as a systematic philosophical method to describe the structures of conscious experience 'as given,' bracketing assumptions about the external world (the 'epoché') to examine how objects appear to consciousness.

Martin Heidegger's 'Being and Time' (1927) asked the 'question of Being' — what does it mean to exist? — and introduced concepts like Dasein (human existence as being-in-the-world), thrownness, and authenticity, fundamentally reshaping 20th-century philosophy.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty's 'Phenomenology of Perception' (1945) challenged Cartesian mind-body dualism by arguing that the body is the very medium of our being-in-the-world, and that perception is an active, embodied engagement rather than a purely intellectual act.

Hermeneutics is the theory of interpretation, originally focused on Biblical and classical texts; Hans-Georg Gadamer's 'Truth and Method' (1960) expanded it to all understanding, arguing that interpretation involves a 'fusion of horizons' between text and interpreter.

Paul Ricoeur synthesized hermeneutics with phenomenology and narrative theory in works like 'Time and Narrative' (1984–88), arguing that the self is constituted through narrative identity — we understand who we are by the stories we tell about ourselves.

American pragmatism, founded by Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, holds that the meaning of any concept lies in its practical consequences and that truth is what works — ideas are tools, not mirrors of reality.

John Dewey (1859–1952) extended pragmatism into education, ethics, and democracy, arguing that learning is an active, experiential process ('learning by doing') and that democracy is not just a political system but a way of associated living.

Richard Rorty's neo-pragmatism in 'Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature' (1979) argued that the mind does not 'mirror' the world, that philosophy should abandon the search for foundations, and that solidarity — our practical commitments to one another — matters more than objectivity.

The analytic-continental divide in 20th-century philosophy roughly separates Anglo-American philosophy (focused on logic, language, and science) from continental European philosophy (focused on human existence, culture, and history); the split emerged around the early 20th century with Frege, Russell, and Moore on one side and Heidegger and Husserl on the other.

Ubuntu philosophy, central to many African ethical traditions, is encapsulated in the Nguni proverb 'Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu' — 'A person is a person through other persons' — emphasizing communal interdependence and humanity constituted through relationships rather than individualism.

African Sage Philosophy, systematized by Henry Odera Oruka in Kenya from the 1970s, identified and documented the philosophical insights of rural, non-literate African sages through in-depth interviews, challenging the assumption that philosophy requires a written tradition.

Kwame Anthony Appiah's 'Cosmopolitanism: Ethics in a World of Strangers' (2006) argues for a philosophy of cosmopolitanism that combines universal ethical obligations to all humans with respect for cultural difference, rejecting both narrow nationalism and imposing cultural uniformity.

Feminist philosophy critiques the gendered assumptions embedded in philosophical traditions and argues that standpoint epistemology — the idea that knowledge is situated and that marginalized perspectives offer epistemic insights — enriches philosophical inquiry.

Simone de Beauvoir's 'The Second Sex' (1949) argued that woman is not born but made: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' — demonstrating how patriarchal society constructs femininity as 'the Other' relative to male subjectivity.

Carol Gilligan's 'In a Different Voice' (1982) challenged Kohlberg's theory of moral development by arguing it reflected male norms; she identified an 'ethics of care' grounded in relationships and context, contrasted with a justice-based 'ethics of rights' — one of feminist philosophy's most influential contributions.

Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' (1990) introduced the concept of gender performativity — the idea that gender is not a fixed identity but is constituted through repeated acts and performances, destabilizing binary conceptions of sex and gender.

Aldo Leopold's 'A Sand County Almanac' (1949) articulated the 'land ethic,' expanding moral consideration beyond humans to include soils, waters, plants, and animals — a foundational text of environmental ethics arguing that 'a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community.'

Deep ecology, developed by Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss in the 1970s, holds that nature has intrinsic value independent of human interests and advocates for a fundamental shift in human-nature relationships — contrasted with 'shallow ecology' which merely addresses environmental problems within an anthropocentric framework.

Peter Singer's 'Animal Liberation' (1975) applied the utilitarian principle of equal consideration of interests to animals, arguing that the capacity to suffer — not species membership — is the morally relevant criterion, launching the modern animal rights movement.

Tom Regan's rights-based approach to animal ethics in 'The Case for Animal Rights' (1983) argued that animals are 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value and thus have rights that cannot be overridden by utilitarian calculation — a deontological complement to Singer's consequentialist approach.

Philosophy of technology, developed by figures including Jacques Ellul and Albert Borgmann, examines how technology shapes human experience and values; Ellul's 'The Technological Society' (1954) argued that technology (la technique) becomes autonomous, reshaping society in its own image.

Nick Bostrom's superintelligence thesis argues that if machines ever surpass human intelligence, the result could be an 'intelligence explosion' leading to an artificial general intelligence that may be indifferent or hostile to human values — making AI alignment the most important philosophical and technical challenge of our era.

John Dewey's philosophy of education argues that schools should reflect democratic values and that education is 'not preparation for life but life itself' — emphasizing problem-solving, creativity, and social participation over rote learning.

Paulo Freire's 'Pedagogy of the Oppressed' (1968) critiqued what he called the 'banking concept' of education — treating students as receptacles for deposited knowledge — and proposed a dialogical, consciousness-raising approach rooted in social critique and liberation.

Immanuel Kant's philosophy of education, outlined in his lectures published posthumously, argued that humans are the only beings needing education to actualize their rationality and moral potential — discipline, culture, civilization, and moralization are the four tasks of education.

Aesthetics as a distinct branch of philosophy was named by Alexander Baumgarten in his 'Aesthetica' (1750), which defined it as the science of sensory knowledge and beauty; Kant's 'Critique of Judgment' (1790) later made aesthetic judgment — the judgment of taste — a central philosophical problem.

Kant's 'Critique of Judgment' argued that judgments of beauty are subjective (based on feeling) yet claim universal assent — we say 'this is beautiful' not 'I like this' — and that the experience of the sublime (overwhelming greatness or power) involves a recognition of our moral nature above nature.

Arthur Danto's 'institutional theory of art' holds that something is a work of art if and only if it is treated as such by the 'art world' — institutions, practices, and theories; his encounter with Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes (1964) prompted this influential analysis.

The paradox of fiction asks how we can genuinely fear Dracula or pity Anna Karenina when we know they don't exist — Kendall Walton resolves this by arguing emotional responses to fiction are 'quasi-emotions' arising from a game of make-believe.

Alvin Plantinga's 'reformed epistemology' argues that belief in God can be properly basic — rationally held without being inferred from other beliefs — just as perceptual and memory beliefs are; this challenges the evidentialist demand that faith requires argument.

William Paley's 'natural theology' argument from design (1802) compared nature to a watch — if you found a watch, you would infer a watchmaker — arguing that the complexity of organisms similarly implies a divine designer; Darwin's theory of natural selection provided the chief scientific rebuttal.

Pascal's Wager (1669) is a pragmatic argument for believing in God: if God exists and you believe, infinite gain; if God exists and you don't believe, infinite loss; since the expected utility of belief is higher regardless of probability, it is rational to believe.

The ontological argument for God's existence, first formulated by Anselm of Canterbury in the 'Proslogion' (1078), argues that since God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' God must exist in reality and not just in the mind — as a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists only as a concept.

Process theology, associated with Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne, argues that God is not unchanging and omnipotent but is in process with the world — affected by creation, growing in experience — offering a response to the problem of evil by limiting divine power.

Analytic philosophy of religion entered a renaissance in the 1970s with Alvin Plantinga, William Alston, and Richard Swinburne applying the tools of analytic philosophy to questions about God, religious experience, and the rationality of faith — reversing the positivist verdict that religious language is meaningless.

The Socratic method — elenchus — systematically questions interlocutors' beliefs to expose contradictions and lead toward greater self-knowledge and truth; its application to professional and institutional life is the basis of modern critical thinking pedagogy.

The moral philosophy of Henry Sidgwick in 'Methods of Ethics' (1874) identified three fundamental ethical methods — egoism, intuitionism, and utilitarianism — and argued that utilitarianism best systematizes our moral intuitions while exposing an unresolved 'dualism of practical reason' between self-interest and universal benevolence.

The ship of Theseus paradox — if all parts of a ship are gradually replaced, is it still the same ship? — has been debated since antiquity as a problem of identity and persistence; Hobbes added a twist: what if someone assembled the original parts into a new ship?

Leibniz's 'principle of sufficient reason' holds that nothing exists without a reason for its existence — for every truth there is a reason why it is so rather than otherwise; it is a foundational principle of rationalist metaphysics and has been applied in cosmological arguments for God.

Derek Parfit's 'Reasons and Persons' (1984) challenged commonsense views about personal identity, rationality, and ethics, arguing that personal identity is not what matters in survival (what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness), generating far-reaching implications for ethics and future generations.

The problem of universals — do abstract properties like 'redness' or 'justice' exist independently of particular things or only as mental concepts? — divides realists (universals are real), nominalists (only particulars exist), and conceptualists (universals are mental concepts).

Continental philosophy's 'linguistic turn' is associated with post-structuralism — Derrida's deconstruction, Foucault's discourse analysis, and Lacan's psychoanalytic linguistics — each arguing in different ways that language and power structure reality and identity.

Jacques Derrida's deconstruction reveals how binary oppositions structuring Western thought (presence/absence, speech/writing, nature/culture) are hierarchical and unstable; his reading of philosophical texts traces how they undermine their own stated arguments.

Michel Foucault's genealogical method, inspired by Nietzsche, examined how power-knowledge systems produce categories of normality and pathology — his histories of madness, medicine, sexuality, and the prison showed how 'truth' reflects specific historical power relations.

The simulation hypothesis, popularized by Nick Bostrom (2003), argues that if it is possible to run simulations of minds, and if many such simulations are run, it is likely that we are ourselves in a simulation — a 21st-century version of Descartes' evil demon.

The Frankfurt cases (Harry Frankfurt, 1969) challenge the principle of alternative possibilities — the idea that moral responsibility requires ability to do otherwise — by describing scenarios where a person would have been compelled to act identically even if they had chosen differently.

Libertarian free will (not the political sense) holds that human choices are genuinely undetermined by prior causes — distinct from both hard determinism (all events are causally necessitated) and compatibilism (freedom is compatible with determinism).

The concept of 'moral luck' (Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams, 1976) points to cases where moral judgment depends on factors beyond our control — the outcome of our actions, circumstances, constitution — undermining the Kantian idea that only intentions determine moral worth.

The epistemic injustice framework, developed by Miranda Fricker in 'Epistemic Injustice' (2007), identifies two main forms: testimonial injustice (discounting someone's testimony due to identity prejudice) and hermeneutical injustice (gaps in collective interpretive resources harming those who lack vocabulary to understand their experience).

Confucianism's concept of ren (benevolence/humaneness) is the central virtue in Confucian ethics — it is cultivated through ritual propriety (li), reciprocity (shu), and the 'golden rule': 'What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others' (Analects 15.24).

Nagarjuna (c. 2nd century CE), founder of the Madhyamaka school of Buddhist philosophy, argued that all phenomena are empty (sunya) of inherent, independent existence — they arise in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designations — a position called sunyata (emptiness).

The Milgram obedience experiments (1961–62), while primarily psychological, have philosophical significance: they showed that ordinary people can be induced to administer what they believe are dangerous electric shocks to strangers, raising philosophical questions about authority, conscience, and the 'banality of evil.'

The naturalistic fallacy, identified by G.E. Moore in 'Principia Ethica' (1903), is the error of defining moral properties (like 'good') in terms of natural properties (like pleasure); Moore argued that 'good' is a simple, unanalyzable, non-natural property.

The 'experience machine' thought experiment by Robert Nozick (1974) asks: would you plug into a machine giving you any desired experiences if it meant you would never leave? Most say no, suggesting that people value reality and authenticity, not just pleasure — a challenge to hedonistic utilitarianism.

The Confucian philosopher Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE) argued that human nature is fundamentally good, citing the instinctive alarm and compassion anyone feels seeing a child about to fall into a well — a moral psychology at odds with Xunzi's view that human nature is bad.

The concept of 'double effect' (Doctrine of Double Effect, originating in Aquinas) permits an action with both good and bad effects if four conditions are met: the action is good in itself, the agent intends only the good effect, the bad effect is not the means to the good, and there is proportionate reason — central to medical ethics and just war theory.

Jean-François Lyotard's 'The Postmodern Condition' (1979) defined postmodernism as 'incredulity toward metanarratives' — suspicion of grand unifying stories like Marxism, Progress, or Enlightenment rationality — shaping postmodern philosophy and cultural theory.

Amartya Sen's capability approach, developed in 'Inequality Reexamined' (1992) and elaborated with Martha Nussbaum, measures human well-being not by utility or income but by what people are able to do and be — their capabilities — providing a richer framework for development ethics.

Iris Murdoch's moral philosophy reinstated the importance of attention (Simone Weil's concept) and vision in ethics, arguing that moral progress consists in learning to see reality more clearly, free from the ego's distortions — a virtue-based approach influenced by Plato and Christianity.

The Trolley Problem, introduced by Philippa Foot (1967) and elaborated by Judith Jarvis Thomson, pits consequentialist and deontological intuitions against each other: would you divert a runaway trolley to kill one person to save five?

Émile Durkheim's sociological philosophy distinguished 'mechanical solidarity' (in traditional societies, based on similarity) from 'organic solidarity' (in modern societies, based on interdependence from division of labor) — influencing both sociology and political philosophy.

The Nyāya school of Indian philosophy, one of six orthodox Hindu philosophical systems, developed one of the ancient world's most sophisticated systems of logic and epistemology, identifying four valid sources of knowledge: perception, inference, comparison, and testimony.

Charles Taylor's 'Sources of the Self' (1989) argued that the modern moral order presupposes tacit background moral ontologies and that the Enlightenment's procedural ethics disastrously separated morality from its motivational sources in moral ideals of the good life.

The philosophical debate over moral realism asks whether moral claims can be objectively true or false; leading moral realists include Derek Parfit and Russ Shafer-Landau, while anti-realists (expressivists like Simon Blackburn and Allan Gibbard) argue moral claims express attitudes rather than describe facts.

The philosophical concept of supervenience, introduced by Donald Davidson in the philosophy of mind, holds that mental properties supervene on physical properties: there can be no mental difference without a physical difference, without requiring identity between mental and physical kinds.

Bertrand Russell's theory of descriptions (1905) resolved puzzles about non-referring phrases like 'the present King of France is bald' — not true (no such king), not false (the negation isn't true either) — by analyzing them as existential quantifier statements with hidden logical form.

The problem of induction, posed by David Hume, asks how we can rationally justify inferring general laws from particular observations; Bertrand Russell illustrated it with the inductivist chicken that expects to be fed every morning until the day it is killed.

Epistemic humility — acknowledging the limits of one's own knowledge — is central to many philosophical traditions from Socrates ('I know that I know nothing') through Nicholas of Cusa's 'docta ignorantia' (learned ignorance) to contemporary fallibilism.

The Eleatic philosophers — Parmenides and Zeno of Elea (c. 490–430 BCE) — argued that change, plurality, and motion are illusions; Zeno's paradoxes (Achilles and the tortoise, the dichotomy) were designed to show that our ordinary sense-experience of motion is logically contradictory.

Hannah Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism in 'The Origins of Totalitarianism' (1951) argued that totalitarian regimes were unprecedented, destroying the political sphere and reducing human beings to superfluous functions, a phenomenon enabled by mass loneliness and rootlessness in modern society.

Martha Nussbaum's 'Upheavals of Thought: The Intelligence of Emotions' (2001) argued that emotions like grief, fear, and compassion are cognitive, laden with evaluative judgments, and not mere disturbances of reason — restoring emotions to their proper place in ethics and philosophy of mind.

The Zhuangzi (c. 4th century BCE) presents Taoist philosophy through parables, arguments, and humor, challenging conventional distinctions between life/death, dream/reality, and self/world; its story of Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly — or a butterfly dreaming it is Zhuangzi — raises questions about identity and perspective.

The contemporary debate on moral status asks which beings merit moral consideration and why — sentience, rationality, relational properties? — with implications for how we treat animals, future persons, artificial intelligences, and those with severe cognitive disabilities.

The Kyoto School philosopher Kitaro Nishida developed the concept of 'basho' (place or topos) as the metaphysical ground of reality — a 'pure experience' prior to the distinction between subject and object — attempting a synthesis of Western and Buddhist-Zen philosophy.

The trolley problem variants — including the footbridge problem (pushing a large man off a bridge to stop the trolley) — reveal that our moral intuitions are inconsistent: most people who would divert the trolley would not push the man, despite similar arithmetic, a finding explored by moral psychology research including Joshua Greene's dual-process model.

Pyrrhonian skepticism, founded by Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BCE), advocated suspension of judgment (epoché) about all matters on the grounds that for every argument there is an equally strong counter-argument — the goal being ataraxia (tranquility of mind).

The analytic tradition's 'ordinary language philosophy,' associated with Gilbert Ryle and the later Wittgenstein at Oxford, argued that philosophical problems arise from misuses of language and can be dissolved — not solved — by carefully attending to how words are ordinarily used.

The Veil of Ignorance thought experiment — from John Rawls' 'A Theory of Justice' (1971) — asks what principles of justice people would choose if they did not know their own social position, talents, or values; it supports Rawls's difference principle that inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged.

Roberto Unger's 'critical legal studies' and 'superliberalism' argue that no social arrangements are natural or necessary — all institutions are frozen politics, contingent choices that can be changed; this voluntarist view underlies his program of 'institutional imagination.'

Pragmatist philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce introduced 'abduction' (inference to the best explanation) as the third form of inference alongside deduction and induction — the creative, hypothesis-generating inference that drives scientific discovery.

Hannah Arendt's concept of the 'banality of evil,' coined in her report on Eichmann's trial ('Eichmann in Jerusalem,' 1963), argued that great evil can be committed by ordinary, 'thoughtless' people who fail to exercise moral judgment and simply follow orders.

Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE), founder of Mohism, challenged Confucian particularist love with 'jian ai' (impartial caring) — equal concern for all persons regardless of relationship — anticipating utilitarian universalism and earning Mohism a place among the 'hundred schools of thought' in ancient China.

The Cartesian circle — a potential circularity in Descartes' argument — is that he uses reason to prove God exists and God's benevolence to validate reason; critics argue this is viciously circular, and Descartes scholars dispute whether and how he escapes this.

Social contract theory's three major versions differ fundamentally: Hobbes (sovereign must be absolute to end the state of war), Locke (government must protect natural rights or may be overthrown), and Rousseau (the general will of the people is sovereign, not any ruler).

The debate between internalism and externalism in epistemology concerns whether the factors that justify a belief must be internally accessible to the believer (internalism) or can be external factors the believer has no access to, such as reliable cognitive processes (reliabilism/externalism).

Plato's 'Allegory of the Cave' in the 'Republic' describes prisoners chained in a cave, seeing only shadows on the wall; philosophy is the process of turning toward the light (the Form of the Good), representing the philosopher's ascent from opinion to knowledge.

The bundle theory of the self, associated with David Hume, holds that there is no persisting self beyond the bundle of perceptions — when he introspected, Hume found only particular perceptions, never a separate 'self' having them.

Analytic philosopher P.F. Strawson argued for 'descriptive metaphysics' — describing the actual structure of our conceptual scheme — rather than 'revisionary metaphysics' (improving on it), arguing in 'Individuals' (1959) that persons and material bodies are the most basic categories of our thought.

Thomas Hobbes's materialist philosophy argued that all reality is composed of matter in motion, including the mind; sensation is caused by external objects pressing on sense organs, initiating motions in the nervous system that constitute our thoughts and feelings.

John Locke's distinction between primary qualities (shape, size, motion — truly in objects) and secondary qualities (color, sound, taste — only in observers' minds) shaped modern philosophy of perception and the debate between direct and indirect realism.

The 'linguistic relativity' hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf hypothesis) proposes that the language we speak influences or determines how we perceive and think about reality; strong versions are largely rejected by linguists, but a weaker claim — that language influences some cognitive patterns — retains empirical support.

The 'knowledge argument' by Frank Jackson (1982) features Mary, a color-blind scientist who knows everything about the physics of color but upon seeing red for the first time learns something new — suggesting that phenomenal consciousness is not reducible to physical facts.

Eliminative materialism, defended by Paul and Patricia Churchland, argues that folk psychological concepts like belief and desire will ultimately be replaced by a mature neuroscience — they are not merely reducible to neuroscience but are fundamentally false descriptions.

The philosophy of time divides into presentism (only the present exists), eternalism (all moments exist equally — the 'block universe'), and growing-block theory (past and present exist, but not the future); Einstein's special relativity is generally taken to favor eternalism.

Giambattista Vico's 'New Science' (1725) was one of the first works to propose a philosophy of history — arguing that human societies pass through recurring ages (divine, heroic, human) and that history is knowable because humans made it ('verum factum' — truth is made).

The cosmological argument for God's existence argues from the existence of the universe to a first cause — Aquinas's Five Ways include versions of this argument, and contemporary philosopher William Lane Craig's 'Kalam cosmological argument' revives it in light of Big Bang cosmology.

The philosophy of mathematics divides into Platonism (mathematical objects exist abstractly and necessarily), formalism (mathematics is a game of symbol manipulation without independent meaning, associated with Hilbert), and intuitionism (mathematics is mental construction, associated with Brouwer).

The concept of 'reflective equilibrium' (John Rawls) describes the process of moving back and forth between moral principles and particular moral judgments, adjusting each in light of the other until they cohere — a method for justifying moral theories.

Emmanuel Levinas's ethics of the 'Other' argues that the encounter with another person's face is the primordial ethical event — the Other's face makes an infinite, unconditional demand on me, placing ethics before ontology as first philosophy.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's concept of 'monads' — simple, soul-like, non-spatial substances without windows (unable to causally interact) — is one of the strangest and most elaborate metaphysical systems in Western philosophy, requiring pre-established harmony ordained by God.

Baruch Spinoza's monism in the 'Ethics' (1677) argued there is only one substance — God or Nature (Deus sive Natura) — with thought and extension as its two known attributes; human beings are finite modes of this one infinite substance.

The 'prisoner's dilemma' in game theory has philosophical implications for ethics and political philosophy: rational self-interest leads to outcomes worse for all parties, illustrating why cooperation requires trust, reputation, and iteration rather than mere rationality.

The concept of 'alienation' in Marx's early writings describes the estrangement workers experience from their labor (the product, the act of production, their species-being, and other workers) under capitalist conditions — a concept that bridges philosophy and social critique.

Aristotle's distinction between potentiality (dunamis) and actuality (energeia) remains one of the most important metaphysical distinctions in Western philosophy, explaining change and motion: what is actual brings what is potential into actuality.

The doctrine of the 'eternal recurrence' in Nietzsche's thought asks: if you had to live your life exactly as it is, over and over, for eternity — would you affirm it? It is meant as both a cosmological hypothesis and an ethical test of whether one truly loves life.

The philosophy of biology examines concepts like species, function, fitness, and teleology; Ernst Mayr distinguished 'proximate causes' (how mechanisms work) from 'ultimate causes' (why evolution shaped them), a distinction central to debates about reducing biology to physics.

The concept of 'extended mind' (Andy Clark and David Chalmers, 1998) argues that cognition can extend beyond the brain and body into the environment — a notebook or smartphone can be literally part of a person's cognitive system if it plays the right functional role.

The Stoic concept of the 'hegemonikon' (ruling faculty) is the rational soul's governing part, responsible for perception, judgment, and assent; Stoic therapy aims to correct false judgments and assents — passions like anger are not feelings but cognitive errors.

Phenomenologist Edmund Husserl's concept of 'intentionality' — that consciousness is always consciousness of something, always directed toward an object — became the central concept of 20th-century continental philosophy of mind.

W.E.B. Du Bois's concept of 'double consciousness' — the sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity — is a foundational contribution to philosophy of race and identity.

The concept of 'imago Dei' (image of God) in Judeo-Christian philosophy grounds human dignity, arguing that humans have intrinsic worth because they are made in God's image; it influenced Kant's categorical imperative and remains central to religious ethics and human rights discourse.

Jean-Paul Sartre's atheistic existentialism argues that 'existence precedes essence' — there is no pre-given human nature or purpose; we are 'condemned to be free,' responsible for creating ourselves and our values through our choices.
