The concept of 'facticity' in existentialist philosophy refers to the given, unchosen aspects of one's existence — body, birth, social class, historical context — that constrain freedom without determining it; Sartre and Beauvoir analyze the tension between facticity and transcendence.

Albert Camus's philosophy of the absurd in 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942) argues that the fundamental question of philosophy is whether life is worth living given the silence of the universe to our demand for meaning; his answer is defiant affirmation despite absurdity.

The philosophy of sport examines whether sport has intrinsic or instrumental value, debates about performance enhancement, the nature of athletic achievement, and whether competitive sport builds or corrupts character — a growing area of applied philosophy.

Bioethics as a distinct field emerged in the 1960s–70s with the creation of the Hastings Center (1969) and the Kennedy Institute of Ethics (1971), responding to new moral dilemmas in medicine including organ transplants, life support, and genetic technologies.

The principlism framework in bioethics (Beauchamp and Childress, 'Principles of Biomedical Ethics,' 1979) identifies four principles: autonomy (respect for patients' decisions), beneficence (doing good), non-maleficence (avoiding harm), and justice (fair distribution of benefits and burdens).

Structural racism — the embeddedness of racial hierarchy in social structures, institutions, and norms — has become a central concept in contemporary philosophy of race, challenging liberal individualism's focus on intentional discrimination.

Cornel West's prophetic pragmatism synthesizes Dewey's pragmatism, Christian theology, and democratic socialism to address the existential crisis of contemporary Black Americans and the nihilism produced by oppression — a distinctive contribution to American philosophy.

David Chalmers's 'zombie' argument holds that it is conceivable — and therefore possible — that there could be beings physically identical to humans but lacking any conscious experience (philosophical zombies), arguing that consciousness cannot be purely physical.

The philosophy of language's 'meaning holism' — Quine and Davidson — holds that the meaning of individual sentences cannot be determined in isolation but only in relation to an entire network of beliefs and sentences; this has implications for radical translation and interpretation.

Positive psychology, influenced by philosopher Aristotle's concept of eudaimonia, argues that human flourishing requires more than the absence of misery — it requires positive emotions, engagement, relationships, meaning, and achievement (Martin Seligman's PERMA model).

Francis Bacon's 'Novum Organum' (1620) proposed replacing Aristotelian logic with an inductive method for natural science, arguing that the mind must be purged of 'idols' (biases) — Idols of the Tribe, Cave, Marketplace, and Theatre — before it can study nature clearly.

Michael Polanyi's concept of 'tacit knowledge' — 'we can know more than we can tell' — identifies a dimension of human expertise and judgment that cannot be fully articulated in explicit rules or propositions, challenging AI optimism and rationalist accounts of knowledge.

The philosophy of religion debate on 'faith and reason' has three main positions: faith is independent of reason (fideism, associated with Kierkegaard), faith is supported by reason (evidentialist theology, Swinburne), and faith is itself rational without needing argumentative support (reformed epistemology, Plantinga).

Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974) argued that the subjective character of experience — what it is like for an organism to be that organism — cannot be captured by objective, third-person scientific description, posing the fundamental challenge to physicalist accounts of mind.

text: The Confucian concept of 'self-cultivation' (xiuqi) is the life-long process of moral and intellectual development — through study, ritual practice, and reflection — toward the ideal of the junzi (exemplary person or gentleman) who embodies virtue and wisdom.

The contemporary philosophy of memory distinguishes episodic memory (remembering personally experienced events), semantic memory (factual knowledge), and procedural memory (skills), examining whether memories are reconstructive, how memory relates to personal identity, and the ethics of memory manipulation.

Pyrrhonian skepticism's criterion problem argues that to judge which things are true, you need a criterion; but to establish which criterion is correct, you need another criterion — leading to an infinite regress or vicious circularity.

George Santayana (1863–1952) is best known for his aphorism 'Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it' from 'The Life of Reason' (1905) — though his philosophy, combining naturalism with aesthetics and a skeptical realism, deserves broader philosophical recognition.

The problem of the external world asks how we can know that an external world of physical objects exists independently of our perceptions; Descartes raised it by imagining an evil demon, Berkeley denied the external world, and Moore famously attempted to refute skepticism by holding up his hands.

Kwame Gyekye's African philosophy defends a moderate form of communitarianism, arguing that while persons are constituted by community, they also have an individual identity and natural rights that the community cannot override — a response to both Western individualism and radical African communitarianism.

The philosophy of language distinction between 'use theory' (meaning as use — Wittgenstein) and 'truth-conditional semantics' (meaning as truth conditions — Davidson and Frege) remains one of the central debates in philosophy of language.

Hellenistic philosophy after Aristotle produced four major schools: Epicureanism (pleasure and tranquility as highest goods), Stoicism (virtue as the only good), Skepticism (suspension of judgment), and Neoplatonism (Plotinus — the One as ultimate reality) — each offering complete ways of life as well as philosophical doctrines.

The philosophical concept of 'umwelt' (environment), developed by biologist Jakob von Uexküll and embraced by phenomenologists, holds that each animal species has its own subjective, species-specific world constituted by its perceptual and action capacities — relevant to animal ethics and environmental philosophy.

The principle of 'non-identity problem' (Derek Parfit) argues that future people whose existence depends on our policies cannot be harmed by those policies — since if we acted differently, they would not exist — posing a deep puzzle for obligations to future generations.

The Analects of Confucius — compiled by his disciples in the 4th or 5th century BCE — contain some of the most quoted philosophical maxims in history; among its themes are the importance of continuous learning, the cultivation of virtue through ritual, and the priority of right relationships.

Intersectionality, coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989), describes how multiple systems of oppression (race, gender, class, sexuality) intersect to create unique and compounding forms of discrimination — a concept that began in legal scholarship and became central to feminist philosophy.

The 'paradox of tolerance' (Karl Popper, 1945) holds that unlimited tolerance must lead to the disappearance of tolerance; to maintain tolerant society, we must be intolerant of intolerance — a philosophical argument with renewed relevance in debates about free speech and hate speech.

text: Gaston Bachelard's 'The Poetics of Space' (1958) examines how intimate spaces (corners, drawers, nests, shells) generate philosophical reverie and argues that the house is not merely a place but a fundamental experience of inhabitation — influencing architectural theory and phenomenology.

The 'swampman' thought experiment (Donald Davidson, 1987) imagines a molecule-for-molecule replica of Davidson created by lightning in a swamp; Davidson argues this being would have no mental content — no beliefs, desires, or meanings — because it lacks the right causal history.

The concept of 'dignity' plays different roles in philosophical traditions: for Kant it is the absolute worth of rational beings grounding the categorical imperative; in Catholic social teaching it underpins human rights; in contemporary bioethics it is contested as sometimes reinforcing rather than extending respect.

Enactivism, developed by Varela, Thompson, and Rosch in 'The Embodied Mind' (1991), argues that cognition is not representation but action — knowledge emerges through embodied engagement with the world, not from computation on inner representations.

Socrates's famous claim that 'the unexamined life is not worth living' (Apology, 38a) encapsulates his commitment to philosophy as a way of life — continuous critical reflection on one's values and beliefs rather than mere pursuit of comfort and success.

Michael Sandel's 'Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?' (2009) popularized philosophical ethics for a mass audience by examining real dilemmas through the lens of utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, and virtue ethics — making it one of the best-selling philosophy books of the 21st century.

The Gettier problem (Edmund Gettier, 1963) showed that justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge by constructing counterexamples where someone has a justified true belief that we would not count as knowledge — spawning decades of epistemological debate on what must be added.

The 'open question argument' by G.E. Moore holds that for any natural property N, it is always an open question whether 'X has N' means 'X is good' — if 'good' were identical to any natural property, this question would be closed like asking if a bachelor is unmarried.

Spinoza's ethical philosophy argued that all human passions stem from inadequate ideas about ourselves and the world; the highest human good is intellectual love of God (amor intellectualis Dei) — understanding that we are modes of an infinite substance — which brings freedom from bondage to passive emotions.

The concept of 'aporetic' dialogues in Plato — 'Euthyphro,' 'Meno,' 'Laches' — end in aporia (perplexity), having failed to define virtue, piety, or knowledge; Socrates regards this as philosophically valuable, as recognizing one's ignorance is the first step toward wisdom.

Logic's modal operators — necessity (□) and possibility (◇) — are studied in modal logic; possible worlds semantics (Saul Kripke and David Lewis) uses the idea of alternative possible worlds to give truth conditions for modal statements.

David Hume's 'is-ought gap' (Treatise, 1739) observed that moral philosophers illicitly move from factual 'is' statements to normative 'ought' statements without justification — a logical gap (later formulated as the naturalistic fallacy by Moore) that remains central to metaethics.

The Mimamsa school of Indian philosophy specializes in the interpretation of the Vedic texts and holds that the Vedas are eternal, authorless, and intrinsically valid — a position called svataḥ prāmāṇya (self-certification of knowledge) that influenced Hindu jurisprudence.

In contemporary philosophy of technology, Albert Borgmann's concept of 'the device paradigm' argues that modern technology conceals its working to deliver commodities (warmth without fire, music without performance), displacing 'focal practices' that center and enrich human life.

The question of moral demandingness — how demanding morality can be before its demands become unreasonable — is raised acutely by Peter Singer's argument that affluent people are obligated to give until they reach marginal utility, drastically curtailing ordinary life.

The philosophy of color asks whether colors are objective properties of objects, subjective responses of perceivers, or dispositions to cause perceptions; the phenomenon of color constancy — we perceive a white page as white under fluorescent and sunlight — complicates purely subjective accounts.

The problem of free will and determinism is sharpened by neuroscientific findings: Benjamin Libet's experiments (1983) showed that brain activity predicting a hand movement begins ~500ms before the subject consciously decides to move, leading some to conclude that conscious will is retrospective.

The philosophical debate on moral relativism divides between descriptive relativism (moral views differ across cultures), metaethical relativism (moral truths are relative to cultures), and normative relativism (we should not judge other cultures' practices) — only the first is widely accepted.

Axiology — the theory of value — studies intrinsic and instrumental value, welfare, and perfectionism; G.E. Moore's 'ideal utilitarianism' holds that beauty and knowledge have intrinsic value alongside pleasure, broadening utilitarian calculation beyond subjective satisfaction.

Heidegger's concept of 'ready-to-hand' (zuhandenheit) and 'present-at-hand' (vorhandenheit) distinguishes tools transparently engaged in smooth activity from objects contemplated detachedly; breakdown (when a hammer breaks) converts the ready-to-hand into the present-at-hand.

Feminist philosopher Sandra Harding developed feminist standpoint epistemology and 'strong objectivity,' arguing that incorporating marginalized perspectives into research actually produces stronger, less partial knowledge than the illusory 'view from nowhere' of traditional objectivity.

The 'Copernican revolution' in philosophy — Kant's term for his own discovery that objects conform to our cognition rather than cognition conforming to objects — means that the structure of experience is partly constituted by the mind's own forms of intuition (space and time) and categories (causality, substance).

The thought experiment of 'Rawls's difference principle' stipulates that social and economic inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society — a principle often cited as a philosophical foundation for welfare-state redistribution.

The Madhyamaka Buddhist philosopher Candrakirti (7th century CE) developed the Prasangika interpretation of Nagarjuna, arguing through reductio ad absurdum that all views — including the view that all views are empty — must be abandoned for liberation.

The philosophy of luck studies 'epistemic luck' (true beliefs formed by accident), 'safety conditions' for knowledge (if things had been different, you would still have believed correctly), and moral luck — questioning how these concepts fit together.

The concept of 'akrasia' (weakness of will) — acting against one's better judgment — puzzled ancient philosophers: Socrates denied it was possible (you always act on what you think is best); Aristotle accepted it as real and analyzed it in the 'Nicomachean Ethics.'

Contemporary analytic metaphysics has revived questions about causation, laws of nature, grounding, and ontological dependence; David Lewis's theory of causation as counterfactual dependence and his modal realism (multiple concrete possible worlds) are among the 20th century's most ambitious and controversial metaphysical systems.

Foucault's concept of 'biopower' describes the modern form of power that targets populations and individual bodies — managing birth rates, health, sexuality, and death through statistical knowledge, public health systems, and normalizing judgments rather than sovereign force.

The concept of 'mana' in Polynesian and Melanesian cultures — spiritual power or authority — has attracted philosophical interest as an indigenous ontological category distinct from Western concepts of soul, fate, or divine will, and relevant to debates about non-Western metaphysics.

The philosophy of death examines whether death is bad for the one who dies (Epicurus said no — after death there is no one to be harmed), whether we can harm future or past persons, and what constitutes the good death — questions central to bioethics and palliative care.

The Nicomachean Ethics' doctrine of the 'mean' (mesotes) holds that virtue is a disposition to feel and act in a way that hits the mean between excess and deficiency relative to us — courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between prodigality and miserliness.

The emergence of cognitive science as a unified discipline in the 1970s–80s brought together philosophy, psychology, linguistics, neuroscience, and AI to study the mind; philosophers like Jerry Fodor played key roles with his 'Language of Thought' hypothesis (1975) about the computational structure of cognition.

The 'paradox of hedonism' holds that making pleasure your direct goal is self-defeating — happiness comes as a by-product of activities and relationships valued for themselves, not as an object of direct pursuit; John Stuart Mill noted that those who are happiest 'have their minds fixed on some other object than their own happiness.'

Alisdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981) argued that modern moral philosophy has collapsed into incoherence because it retains the vocabulary of virtue ethics and duty while abandoning the Aristotelian teleological framework that gave those concepts their rational grounding.

The problem of other minds asks how we can know that other people have minds and conscious experiences rather than being philosophical zombies; Wittgenstein's private language argument shows that even the concept of one's own inner life requires public, behavioral criteria.

The French philosopher Simone Weil's concept of 'affliction' (malheur) describes extreme suffering that crushes the soul and destroys the self — it is distinct from ordinary pain and requires not compassion (which recognizes the sufferer) but a specific form of attention that fully acknowledges their existence.

The Vedantic concept of 'Brahman-Atman identity' in Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism), systematized by Adi Shankaracharya (8th century CE), holds that the ultimate reality (Brahman) and the individual self (Atman) are identical; all apparent multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Pragmatist philosopher William James argued in 'The Will to Believe' (1897) that in certain conditions — where the choice is momentous, forced, and living, and where evidence cannot decide — it is rational to believe on the basis of emotional and volitional considerations rather than evidence.

The philosophical problem of social ontology asks what kind of thing social entities — money, marriage, corporations, governments — are; John Searle's 'Construction of Social Reality' (1995) argues they are objective but dependent on collective intentionality and status functions.

Confucian philosopher Xunzi (c. 310–235 BCE) held a view antithetical to Mencius — that human nature is bad (xing e) and that morality is not the actualization of inherent goodness but the product of education, ritual, and conscious effort (wei).

The feminist philosopher Patricia Collins developed 'matrix of domination' as a framework showing how race, class, gender, and sexuality intersect as interlocking systems of oppression rather than additive categories — building on but extending Crenshaw's intersectionality.

The mind-body problem's central positions include dualism (Descartes: mind and body are distinct substances), physicalism/materialism (only physical things exist), and property dualism (one substance with two kinds of properties — physical and mental); the latter is currently the most common compromise position.

The Indian philosopher Dignaga (5th century CE) founded the Epistemological (Pramana) school of Buddhist philosophy, making perception and inference the only valid sources of knowledge; his work influenced not only Buddhist but also Hindu epistemology.

The philosophy of humor has three main theories: superiority theory (laughter at others' inferiority — Hobbes), incongruity theory (humor arises from violations of expectation — Kant and Schopenhauer), and relief theory (humor releases nervous energy — Freud).

The ancient Indian text 'Arthashastra' (c. 4th century BCE), attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), is both a manual for statecraft and a work of political philosophy; its sophisticated analysis of power, war, diplomacy, and administration is comparable to Machiavelli's 'The Prince.'

The philosophical concept of 'authenticity,' central to existentialism (Heidegger, Sartre), describes genuinely owning one's existence — choosing, acting, and living in accordance with one's own values rather than fleeing into the impersonal 'they-self' (das Man) through conformity and distraction.

Plato's theory of recollection (anamnesis), presented in the 'Meno' and 'Phaedo,' argues that learning is actually remembering — the soul knew the Forms before birth and philosophy helps it recollect this knowledge, suggesting that all knowledge is a priori.

The Epicurean argument that 'death is nothing to us' (Epicurus, 'Letter to Menoeceus') rests on the symmetry between prenatal and posthumous non-existence: we were not troubled by not existing before birth, so we should not fear not existing after death.

The philosophical literature on consent distinguishes valid consent (informed, voluntary, competent) from mere agreement; issues about consent permeate bioethics, sexual ethics, political legitimacy, and contract law — making it one of applied philosophy's most cross-cutting concepts.

The Stoic 'sage' (sophos) — the perfectly virtuous, fully rational person — is an ideal almost no one achieves; the Stoics acknowledged this while holding that wisdom is all-or-nothing, making every non-sage equally foolish, a doctrine that struck even ancient critics as paradoxical.

The concept of 'alterity' (otherness) in continental philosophy — developed by Levinas, Derrida, and Bhabha — examines how the encounter with radical difference constitutes the self and raises ethical responsibilities to those who cannot be assimilated to our categories.

Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792) is one of the earliest works of feminist philosophy, arguing that women's apparent inferiority is produced by their lack of education and rational development — not natural difference — and demanding equal educational opportunities.

Bertrand Russell's famous teapot analogy argues that the burden of proof lies with those making unfalsifiable claims: if he claimed there is a teapot orbiting the sun too small to be detected, he could not demand that others disprove it — a challenge to requiring disproof of God's existence.

The Chinese philosopher Wang Yangming (1472–1529) developed a school of Neo-Confucianism emphasizing 'unity of knowledge and action' (zhixing heyi): genuine knowledge necessarily results in action, so those who know the good but do not act are not yet truly knowing.

The philosophical concept of 'emergence' holds that systems have properties that their parts lack and that cannot be predicted from knowledge of the parts alone; strong emergence (consciousness from brain matter) is controversial, while weak emergence (wetness from H2O molecules) is widely accepted.

The idea of 'philosophical therapy' — philosophy as a cure for psychic disturbance — runs through Epicurus, Stoicism, and Pyrrhonism in antiquity, and has been revived by philosophers like Pierre Hadot and Martha Nussbaum who see ancient philosophy as fundamentally practical.

Nelson Goodman's 'grue' paradox (1955) shows that inductive logic has a 'new riddle': 'grue' (green before a certain time, then blue) satisfies all past evidence as well as 'green,' but seems an unprojectible predicate, raising the question of which properties support genuine inductive generalizations.

The concept of 'thick' moral concepts — cowardly, cruel, brave, kind — are both descriptive and evaluative, unlike 'thin' concepts (good, right) that are purely evaluative; their existence is used both to challenge the fact-value distinction and to argue for virtue ethics.

The problem of moral motivation — what motivates us to act morally — divides internalists (moral judgments necessarily motivate) from externalists (the connection between judgment and motivation is contingent); Hume's view that reason is the slave of the passions makes him a motivational externalist.

Consequentialism's 'repugnant conclusion' (Parfit) holds that for any large number of happy people, there is a larger population whose lives are barely worth living whose existence would be better — challenging population ethics with a deeply counterintuitive result.

Phenomenological psychiatry, influenced by Husserl and Heidegger, analyzes mental disorders as alterations in the fundamental structure of experience — space, time, body, and intersubjectivity — rather than as brain dysfunctions alone, offering a humanistic complement to biomedical psychiatry.

The Confucian tradition of 'remonstrance' — the duty of officials to criticize rulers who act unjustly — is one of the earliest philosophical justifications for speaking truth to power; it shaped Chinese political culture and contrasts with Western traditions of individual rights.

The contemporary philosophy of race asks whether race is biological (racial naturalism), socially constructed (racial constructivism), or eliminable (racial eliminativism); most philosophers accept some form of constructivism, holding that race is real as a social category even though biological races do not exist.

Walter Benjamin's 'Theses on the Philosophy of History' (1940) argued that history must be read against the grain, attending to the voices of the defeated and oppressed rather than the victors' narrative; the 'angel of history' is blown forward by the storm of progress while looking back at the wreckage.

The Daoist concept of 'wu wei' (non-action or effortless action) does not mean passivity but rather acting in accordance with the natural flow of things — the sage ruler governs so lightly that the people think they accomplished everything themselves.

The concept of 'moral progress' asks whether there is such a thing — the abolition of slavery, extension of rights to women and LGBTQ+ people, and animal welfare reform suggest there is; Peter Singer and Joshua Greene examine what drives it and whether it has a direction.

The philosophical method of 'conceptual analysis' — breaking down complex concepts into necessary and sufficient conditions — was the dominant methodology of 20th-century analytic philosophy before Gettier's counterexamples and Wittgenstein's family resemblance concept undermined its prospects.

The field of 'experimental philosophy' (x-phi) uses empirical psychological methods — surveys and experiments — to study ordinary people's philosophical intuitions, questioning whether professional philosophers' intuitions are reliable guides to philosophical truth.

David Hume's 'bundle theory' of causation holds that causal necessity is not observed in the world but is a habit of the mind projected onto regular successions of events — 'constant conjunction' is the only empirical basis for causation.

The Renaissance philosopher Pico della Mirandola's 'Oration on the Dignity of Man' (1486) declared that humans have no fixed nature but are free to become whatever they choose — anticipating existentialist themes by 450 years and marking a key moment in humanist philosophy.

The 'communitarian' critique of liberalism by Michael Sandel, Charles Taylor, and Alasdair MacIntyre argues that liberal political theory wrongly treats the self as 'unencumbered' — prior to and independent of its social roles and community — ignoring that identity is constituted by one's communal attachments.

The Japanese aesthetic concept of 'mono no aware' (the pathos of things) describes a bittersweet awareness of the transience of all things — exemplified by the beauty of cherry blossoms that fall quickly — central to Japanese aesthetics and discussed by philosophers including Motoori Norinaga.

In Indian philosophy, the concept of 'karma' (action) in its philosophical sense — not just cosmic justice but the metaphysical mechanism by which intentional actions shape future states of the self — is central to Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain ethics.

The philosophical debate about 'moral intuitions' asks whether they are reliable evidence for moral truths (as in reflective equilibrium) or merely evolved psychological dispositions that may systematically mislead (as some evolutionary debunkers argue).

The Stoic concept of 'oikeiosis' (appropriation or familiarization) describes how humans have a natural affinity first for themselves, then for family, community, and finally all humanity — a philosophical basis for cosmopolitan ethics grounded in human nature rather than abstract reason.

The philosophy of photography, examined by Susan Sontag in 'On Photography' (1977) and Roland Barthes in 'Camera Lucida' (1980), explores whether photographs represent reality (indexical signs) or construct it; Barthes's concept of the 'punctum' (the detail that wounds the viewer) became a touchstone of aesthetic theory.

The 'Fregean' approach to the philosophy of mathematics — logicism — holds that arithmetic is reducible to pure logic; Frege's 'Grundgesetze der Arithmetik' was shown by Russell's paradox to be inconsistent, but neo-logicism (Crispin Wright) attempts to revive a modified version.

The distinction between 'agent-relative' and 'agent-neutral' reasons is central to contemporary ethics: agent-neutral reasons apply equally to everyone (e.g., minimize suffering), while agent-relative reasons favor special obligations to one's own projects and relationships — a key difference between consequentialism and deontology.

The Scottish Enlightenment philosopher Adam Smith's 'Theory of Moral Sentiments' (1759) — less famous than 'The Wealth of Nations' — argues that moral judgments are grounded in sympathy: we judge others by imagining ourselves as an 'impartial spectator' of their situation.

The concept of 'epistemic injustice' has spawned the related concept of 'testimonial smothering' (Kristie Dotson) — the practice of truncating one's testimony to fit what an audience is able to receive — showing how injustice can operate through self-censorship rather than direct silencing.

The 'experience machine' and similar thought experiments ('utility monster,' 'experience machine,' 'transplant case') are tools for testing ethical theories against our intuitions; their power comes from designing cases that isolate key variables to reveal what we really value.

Leo Strauss argued that philosophers writing under political or religious persecution used a 'double writing' technique — an exoteric message for the masses and an esoteric message for careful readers — shaping his influential school of political philosophy at Chicago.

The Madhva school of Dvaita (dualist) Vedanta, founded by Madhvacharya (13th century CE), explicitly rejects Shankara's non-dualism, arguing that God (Brahman/Vishnu), souls, and the world are fundamentally distinct and that devotion (bhakti) is the path to liberation.

The debate about 'moral realism' is inextricably connected to the debate about 'moral motivation': if moral facts are mind-independent, how do they motivate us to act? This 'motivational gap' leads many realists to posit a special faculty of moral intuition or to accept a form of externalism.

Blaise Pascal's distinction between the 'esprit de géométrie' (geometrical mind — reasoning from explicit axioms) and the 'esprit de finesse' (subtle mind — sensitive to complex particulars) captures two modes of rational understanding that both Descartes and Pascal see as legitimate.

Wabi-sabi, a Japanese aesthetic philosophy, finds beauty in imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness — the tea ceremony master Sen no Rikyu (1522–1591) made it a philosophy of life through the concept of 'ichi-go ichi-e' (one time, one meeting).

The concept of 'reflective stability' in Rawls's political philosophy holds that a well-ordered society's principles of justice must be ones that citizens can affirm on reflection, taking into account their deepest values and the constraints of being a fair scheme of cooperation.

The Nyaya-Vaisheshika philosophical alliance in classical Indian philosophy combined Nyaya's logic and epistemology with Vaisheshika's ontology of atoms and categorical substance — an early analytic metaphysics arguing that the world consists of ultimate, indivisible atoms.

The concept of 'care ethics,' developed from Gilligan by Nel Noddings and Joan Tronto, has been applied beyond moral philosophy to politics, arguing that a 'politics of care' should replace competitive individualism with attention to vulnerability, dependency, and relationships.

The Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid's 'common sense philosophy' countered Humean skepticism by arguing that certain basic beliefs — in an external world, in other minds, in memory — are not inferred from experience but are immediate, instinctive, and epistemologically foundational.

The 'transcendental argument' strategy in philosophy — arguing from the conditions of possibility of experience to what must be true — is Kant's central contribution to epistemology and has been applied in defense of free will (Kant), other minds, and morality by subsequent philosophers.

Schopenhauer's aesthetics held that music is unique among the arts in not representing the world of phenomena but directly expressing the will itself — the inner nature of reality — making music the highest art and anticipating Nietzsche's and Wagner's philosophy of music.

The question of whether machines can be conscious is related to but distinct from whether they can be intelligent; integrated information theory (Giulio Tononi) proposes phi (Φ) as a measure of consciousness applicable to any system — potentially including computers.

The philosophical category of 'the uncanny' (das Unheimliche), analyzed by Freud (1919) and Heidegger (as anxiety in the face of non-being), describes the eerie experience of familiar things becoming strange — relevant to literature, art, AI (uncanny valley), and philosophy of mind.

The debate about 'moral psychology' in Kantian ethics centers on whether morality requires acting from the motive of duty alone (pure duty ethics) or whether inclinations and emotions can play a supporting role; Barbara Herman and Christine Korsgaard have offered influential neo-Kantian views.

The 'principle of charity' in philosophy of language (Davidson) holds that we should interpret speakers' utterances in the most rational and consistent way possible — maximizing agreement and rationality — as a constraint on radical translation and interpretation.

Social epistemology examines how social processes and institutions affect knowledge production and distribution; Miranda Fricker, Helen Longino, and Alvin Goldman have shown that testimony, peer disagreement, and group belief are not merely social phenomena but have deep epistemological implications.

The existentialist concept of 'bad faith' (mauvaise foi) in Sartre describes the human tendency to deny one's freedom by treating oneself as a thing — a role, a nature, a facticity — rather than as a being that exists before its essence and is responsible for self-creation.

The field of 'philosophy of psychiatry' examines whether mental disorders are value-neutral biological facts or partly normative constructs; debates about DSM categories, the concept of disorder, and the relationship between neuroscience and clinical practice involve deep philosophical questions.

Antonio Gramsci's concept of 'hegemony' explains how dominant classes maintain power not through force alone but through cultural dominance — making ruling-class ideology appear as common sense; challenging hegemony requires building counter-hegemonic 'organic intellectuals.'

The Indian school of Carvaka (Lokayata) was an ancient materialist and skeptical philosophy rejecting Vedic authority, denying karma and liberation, and holding that only direct perception is a valid source of knowledge — one of the few ancient atheistic-materialist traditions outside the West.

The concept of 'narrative ethics' argues that moral deliberation and character are fundamentally narrative in form — we understand who we are and what we owe others through the stories we inhabit, as argued by Alasdair MacIntyre, Paul Ricoeur, and Martha Nussbaum.

The concept of 'qualia' refers to the subjective, felt qualities of conscious experience — the redness of red, the painfulness of pain — that many philosophers argue cannot be reduced to functional or physical descriptions, posing the central challenge of the hard problem of consciousness.

The 'measurement problem' in quantum mechanics — how the wave function collapses when observed — has generated philosophical debates about the role of observation and the ontological status of the quantum world; interpretations include Copenhagen, Many Worlds, and Bohmian mechanics.

The concept of 'political obligation' asks why citizens have a duty to obey the law; natural duty theories (Rawls), fair play theories (Hart), and associative obligation theories (Dworkin) give different answers, while philosophical anarchists deny there is any general obligation to obey.

In the philosophy of language, 'contextualism' holds that the semantic content of many sentences depends on context of utterance — including 'know' (which may set different evidential standards in different contexts), generating debates about how to account for our intuitions about knowledge attributions.

The concept of 'philosophical zombies' implies that there is an explanatory gap between physical facts and phenomenal consciousness; even if we knew everything about the brain, we would still face the question why those processes are accompanied by experience at all.

The contemporary 'attention economy' raises philosophical questions about manipulation, autonomy, and well-being that connect philosophy of technology, ethics, and political philosophy; Yves Citton and others argue that attention has become the scarce resource of the information age.

The concept of 'epistemic autonomy' — thinking for oneself, forming beliefs through one's own reasoning rather than deference — is both individually valuable and raises social epistemological questions about when deference to experts is appropriate and when it undermines autonomy.

The African philosophical concept of 'hunhu/ubuntu' (Zimbabwe/South Africa) proposes that a person achieves full humanity through their relationships and moral character — 'I am because we are' — offering a communitarian vision of personhood contrasting with Western liberal individualism.

Moral particularism (Jonathan Dancy) holds that the moral relevance of any feature of a situation can vary from case to case — what makes an action wrong in one case may make it right in another — challenging the universalist assumption that ethics requires exceptionless principles.

The philosophical tradition of 'civil disobedience,' from Thoreau's 'Resistance to Civil Government' (1849) to Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963), argues that citizens have not only the right but sometimes the duty to disobey unjust laws through public, nonviolent, and conscientious action.

The Zen Buddhist tradition of koan practice — meditating on paradoxical questions like 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' — is not a philosophical argument but an anti-discursive practice designed to break habitual conceptual thinking and induce direct, non-dualistic experience.

The 'philosophy of forgiveness' examines whether forgiveness is always a virtue, whether it is possible to forgive the unrepentant, and how it relates to justice and memory; Jeffrie Murphy and Charles Griswold have argued that forgiveness properly requires certain conditions from the wrongdoer.

The concept of 'mereology' — the logic of parts and wholes — examines questions like whether ordinary objects (ships, trees, people) are mereological sums of their parts, and whether any arbitrary collection of objects forms a mereological sum; David Lewis's mereological universalism holds that any objects whatsoever compose a further object.

The philosophy of humor's incongruity theory has been refined by noting that not all incongruity is funny — it must be perceived with a specific attitude of 'amused detachment' (Mike Carroll) rather than threat or disgust, suggesting that the emotional framing of incongruity is as important as its presence.

The Aztec philosophical tradition developed a concept of 'teotl' — a dynamic, dual, self-generating sacred force — as the ultimate reality, analyzed by James Maffie as a form of process monism comparable to certain Western and Eastern metaphysical systems.

The 'vicious circle principle,' formulated by Russell and Poincaré to avoid paradoxes in set theory, holds that collections cannot contain members defined in terms of the collection itself — a forerunner of the theory of types and the distinction between levels of language.

The 'lifeworld' (Lebenswelt) concept, introduced by Husserl and developed by Habermas, refers to the pre-theoretical world of shared meanings, practices, and assumptions that forms the background horizon of all human activity — and whose colonization by 'system rationality' Habermas diagnoses as a modern social pathology.

The philosophy of forgiveness is distinct from the philosophy of excuse (reducing blameworthiness) and justification (making the act right); forgiving someone requires holding them responsible while choosing to release resentment — making forgiveness philosophically complex.

The concept of 'cognitive bias' — systematic errors in judgment like availability bias, confirmation bias, and anchoring — raises philosophical questions about epistemic rationality and whether human cognition is fundamentally irrational or rational-within-constraints.

The Analytic philosophy debate on 'abstract objects' — numbers, propositions, types — divides Platonists (they exist independently of minds) from nominalists (only concrete particulars exist) and fictionalists (talk of abstract objects is useful fiction without ontological commitment).

G.W. Leibniz's 'identity of indiscernibles' (Principle of the Identity of Indiscernibles) holds that no two distinct entities share exactly the same properties — if A and B are numerically distinct, they must differ qualitatively; it has been challenged by thought experiments involving qualitatively identical but numerically distinct objects.

The philosophy of 'forgetting' — recently developed by Viktor Mayer-Schönberger in a legal context and philosophers in relation to digital memory — explores whether the right to be forgotten serves autonomy and identity or undermines accountability and historical truth.

The concept of 'moral residue' (Bernard Williams) describes the agent's persistent regret after making a tragic moral choice between two obligations — even when the right choice was made, the unmet obligation leaves a remainder that demands acknowledgment.

The philosopher Ruth Chang's work on 'parity' argues that some value comparisons resist the trichotomy of better, worse, or equally good — two options can be 'on a par,' close in value but neither superior to nor equal with the other, requiring a fourth value relation.

Philosophy of technology thinker Langdon Winner's 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?' (1980) argued that some technologies are inherently political — Robert Moses's low bridges over Long Island parkways were designed to prevent buses (used by Black residents) from accessing Jones Beach, embedding racial politics in infrastructure.

Nishida Kitaro's later philosophy developed the concept of 'absolute nothingness' (zettai mu) as the ground of reality — going beyond the relative nothingness of particular things to a nothingness that is prior to the being-nothingness distinction itself, drawing on Zen Buddhist insights.

The 'genetic fallacy' in logic holds that you cannot evaluate the truth of a claim by pointing to its origins — the origins of an idea (dream, bias, bad upbringing) are irrelevant to whether it is true; this is frequently conflated with legitimate genealogical critiques that show how a concept serves power.

The concept of 'intellectual virtue' — epistemic virtues like open-mindedness, intellectual courage, and humility — was developed by Linda Zagzebski and others in virtue epistemology, shifting the epistemological focus from belief properties to properties of knowers.

The 'conceivability-possibility' argument strategy — arguing from conceivability of X to possibility of X — is widely used but disputed; David Chalmers defends it for consciousness, while critics argue that conceivability at best gives prima facie evidence for possibility, not entailment.

The concept of 'solidarity' has received renewed philosophical attention from Richard Rorty (as the basis of liberal politics), Sally Scholz (social, civic, and political solidarity), and Jodi Dean (political solidarity as the primary commitment among those with shared political goals).

The 'demandingness objection' to utilitarianism holds that if we must always maximize aggregate welfare, we are required to sacrifice almost everything for strangers — leaving no space for personal projects, relationships, or life plans — a critique Samuel Scheffler responds to with 'agent-centered prerogatives.'

The concept of 'care for the self' (epimeleia heautou) in Hellenistic philosophy — examined by Foucault in 'The Care of the Self' (1984) — was a central practice in Stoic, Epicurean, and Pythagorean traditions: philosophy as a way of shaping, examining, and cultivating the self.

The contemporary debate about 'free speech' in political philosophy has moved beyond Mill's harm principle to examine epistemic arguments (free speech produces truth), democratic arguments (self-governance requires open debate), and arguments from autonomy (censorship infantilizes citizens).

The philosophical concept of 'testimony' asks how knowledge is transmitted from one person to another through assertions; reductionists (Hume) hold that testimony is only justified when we have independent reason to trust the testifier, while anti-reductionists hold that testimony generates justified belief by default.

The 'is-ought distinction' is at the heart of contemporary metaethics; moral naturalists deny the distinction (moral facts are natural facts), expressivists deny that moral claims are genuine assertions at all, and error theorists (J.L. Mackie) hold that moral claims are genuine assertions but all false.

The 'autonomy of ethics' thesis holds that moral principles are not derived from religion, metaphysics, or natural science but stand on their own rational footing; it underlies Kant's ethics and modern liberal political philosophy's separation of the right from the good.

The concept of 'framing effects' in moral psychology — where identical options elicit different choices depending on how they are described (as gains vs. losses, killing vs. letting die) — raises philosophical questions about the reliability of moral intuitions as evidence.

Hegel's 'Philosophy of Right' (1820) developed the concept of 'Sittlichkeit' (ethical life) as the concrete actualization of freedom in family, civil society, and the state — distinguishing it from abstract right (property) and morality (conscience), and arguing that persons become truly free only in community.

The philosophical critique of 'essentialism' — the view that natural kinds or social categories have necessary, defining essences — runs through analytic philosophy (Kripke vs. Quine) and feminist and postcolonial philosophy, where essentialism about gender and race is seen as politically dangerous.

The concept of 'animal cognition' and its philosophical implications — do animals have beliefs, desires, intentions, or consciousness? — has been explored by philosophers Donald Griffin, Daniel Dennett, and Mark Rowlands, with implications for animal ethics and the nature of mind.

The debate between 'wide' and 'narrow' content in philosophy of mind asks whether the content of mental states is determined solely by what is in the head (narrow) or partly by the environment and social context (wide); Putnam's Twin Earth argument supports wide content.

The Madhyamaka doctrine of 'two truths' — conventional truth (the everyday world) and ultimate truth (emptiness of inherent existence) — attempts to reconcile ordinary discourse with the philosophical discovery that all things lack intrinsic nature.

David Hume's 'missing shade of blue' — if you have seen all shades of blue except one, can you imagine the missing shade without experiencing it? — is a potential counterexample to Hume's own principle that all simple ideas derive from impressions, acknowledged but set aside by Hume himself.

The contemporary philosophy of emotions has moved from the James-Lange theory (emotions are perceptions of bodily changes) through cognitive appraisal theories (emotions are value judgments — Nussbaum, Lazarus) to pluralist accounts combining cognitive, phenomenal, and physiological elements.

Heraclitus (c. 535–475 BCE) argued that reality is fundamentally characterized by flux and opposition — 'you cannot step into the same river twice' — and that the hidden unity of opposites (the Logos) underlies all apparent change and conflict.

The Platonic concept of 'methexis' (participation) explains how particular things relate to the Forms: a beautiful painting is beautiful because it participates in the Form of Beauty — though Plato himself raised the 'Third Man Argument' as an objection to this account.

Aristotle's four causes — material (what something is made of), formal (its structure or pattern), efficient (what brought it about), and final (its purpose or end) — provide a comprehensive framework for explaining natural and artificial things that dominated Western thought until the Scientific Revolution.

Epicurus taught that the gods have no concern for human affairs and that natural phenomena should be explained without recourse to divine intervention — a philosophical naturalism that aimed to liberate people from the fear of death and divine punishment.

The Stoic doctrine of 'cosmopolitanism' — that all human beings are citizens of a single world city governed by reason — was articulated by Zeno of Citium and became influential through Marcus Aurelius's 'Meditations' and modern theories of global justice.

John Locke's 'Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) argued against innate ideas and for the mind as a 'tabula rasa' — a blank slate written upon by experience — establishing empiricism as a systematic alternative to Cartesian rationalism.

George Berkeley's idealism ('esse est percipi' — to be is to be perceived) denied the existence of mind-independent matter, arguing that physical objects are collections of ideas in minds — including God's mind, which ensures that unperceived objects continue to exist.

Immanuel Kant's 'Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) formulates the categorical imperative in three versions: act only according to maxims you could universalize, treat humanity never merely as a means but always also as an end, and act as a legislating member of a kingdom of ends.

Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832), founder of utilitarianism, argued that 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number is the foundation of morals and legislation' and invented the 'felicific calculus' — a method for measuring pleasures and pains by intensity, duration, certainty, and other dimensions.

John Stuart Mill refined utilitarianism in 'Utilitarianism' (1863) by distinguishing higher pleasures (intellectual and moral) from lower pleasures (bodily), famously arguing that 'it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.'

G.W.F. Hegel's dialectical method — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — describes how thought and history develop through the resolution of contradictions; his 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) traces the journey of consciousness toward Absolute Knowledge.

Arthur Schopenhauer's 'The World as Will and Representation' (1818) argued that the underlying reality of all phenomena is an irrational, insatiable 'Will' — the source of all suffering — and that aesthetic contemplation and asceticism offer the only escapes from its tyranny.

Søren Kierkegaard's 'stages on life's way' describes three modes of existence: the aesthetic stage (pleasure and immediacy), the ethical stage (duty and universal norms), and the religious stage (a personal, paradoxical leap of faith beyond ethics — as in Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac).

Friedrich Nietzsche's concept of the 'Übermensch' (Overman or Superman) is not a racial or political ideal but a philosophical challenge: to create new values beyond the inherited Christian-moral framework after the 'death of God' — a person who masters themselves and affirms life.

William James's 'radical empiricism' went beyond traditional empiricism by including relations — conjunctions, disjunctions, and transitions between experiences — as directly experienced, not merely inferred, making experience a richer and more continuous fabric than Hume's atomic impressions.

Bertrand Russell's logical atomism — developed with Wittgenstein — held that language and thought are composed of logically independent atomic propositions corresponding to atomic facts in the world, and that philosophy's task is to reveal this logical structure beneath surface grammar.

Ludwig Wittgenstein's 'Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus' (1921) argued that the world is the totality of facts, that language pictures facts, and that what cannot be said — ethics, aesthetics, the meaning of life — must be passed over in silence ('Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent').

The Vienna Circle's logical positivism applied the verification principle — that a statement is meaningful only if it is empirically verifiable or analytically true — to eliminate metaphysics; A.J. Ayer's 'Language, Truth and Logic' (1936) popularized this view in English.

The philosopher Simone de Beauvoir argued in 'The Ethics of Ambiguity' (1947) that existentialist freedom is inherently intersubjective — genuine freedom cannot be achieved in isolation but only through relations with others whose freedom one must also affirm.

The Frankfurt School's 'dialectic of enlightenment' (Adorno and Horkheimer, 1944) argued that the Enlightenment's drive to master nature through reason turned against itself — becoming a new form of domination and irrationality in fascism and the culture industry.

Donald Davidson's 'anomalous monism' (1970) argues that mental events are identical with physical events (monism), but mental descriptions cannot be reduced to physical laws (anomalism) — thus preserving the normativity and rationality of the mental while accepting physicalism.

The philosophy of 'social facts' — analyzed by Searle, Durkheim, and contemporary social ontologists — asks how institutions like money, governments, and marriages exist, distinguishing 'brute facts' (observer-independent) from 'institutional facts' (depending on collective acceptance).

Parmenides of Elea (c. 515–450 BCE) argued in his poem 'On Nature' that genuine reality is one, eternal, unchanging, and indivisible — change and multiplicity are illusory — because 'it is impossible to think or speak of non-being,' and all change requires something coming from non-being.

Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE) founded a religious-philosophical community that held that numbers are the ultimate reality — numerical ratios govern music, astronomy, and the cosmos — and that the soul is immortal and undergoes metempsychosis (transmigration into new bodies).

Empedocles (c. 494–434 BCE) proposed that all matter is composed of four 'roots' (earth, water, fire, air) and that the universe alternates between a state of unity under Love (Philia) and a state of separation under Strife (Neikos) — an early cosmological theory of cyclical change.

The Sophists — professional teachers of rhetoric in ancient Athens including Protagoras and Gorgias — questioned objective truth and morality; Protagoras's claim that 'man is the measure of all things' is the earliest formulation of relativism about knowledge and value.

The Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BCE) rejected social conventions and material possessions, living in a barrel and reportedly telling Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight — embodying the Cynic ideal of virtue as the only good and nature as the guide to life.

The Megarian school of logic, associated with Diodorus Cronus and Philo of Megara (4th century BCE), made important contributions to propositional logic and conditionals — anticipating aspects of modern logic that would not be fully developed until the Stoics and 19th-century logicians.

Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE–50 CE) synthesized Jewish scripture with Platonic philosophy, interpreting the Torah allegorically and identifying the Platonic Logos with the divine intermediary through which God created the world — influencing later Christian and Islamic philosophy.

Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 CE) wrote 'Isagoge' — an introduction to Aristotle's Categories — which raised the 'problem of universals' by asking whether species and genera exist independently or only in the mind; this question dominated medieval philosophy for centuries.

John Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877 CE) was one of medieval Europe's most original philosophers, translating Pseudo-Dionysius and developing a Neoplatonic Christian theology in 'Periphyseon' — arguing that God, as the totality of being, is both creator and creation.

The Islamic philosopher Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 CE), often called 'the first Arab philosopher,' sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Islamic theology and argued that philosophy (the pursuit of truth) and religion (revealed truth) must ultimately agree, since truth is one.

Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037 CE) developed the 'Floating Man' thought experiment — a person suspended in air, deprived of all sensory input — and argued that this person would still be aware of their own existence as a thinking self, independently of the body, anticipating Descartes' cogito.

Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198 CE), known as 'The Commentator' in medieval Europe, wrote detailed commentaries on Aristotle and argued forcefully for the compatibility of philosophy and Islam — his works, translated into Latin, sparked the Averroist movement in medieval Christian universities.

Peter Abelard (1079–1142 CE) developed 'conceptualism' as a middle position in the universals debate — universals are neither independently existing realities (realism) nor merely words (nominalism), but mental concepts (conceptus) abstracted from individual things.

Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464) developed 'docta ignorantia' (learned ignorance) — the recognition that God's infinite nature surpasses all human concepts and that the wisest knowledge is knowing the limits of one's knowledge — anticipating later negative theology and epistemological humility.

Francis Suárez (1548–1617), the great Jesuit scholastic philosopher, developed the doctrine of 'haecceity' and argued in 'Disputationes Metaphysicae' that being is univocal — applying in the same sense to God and creatures — influencing both Descartes and Leibniz.

The Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire's 'Candide' (1759) satirized Leibniz's philosophical optimism ('all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds') through a series of disasters, reflecting the philosophical crisis prompted by the Lisbon earthquake of 1755.

The Scottish Enlightenment philosopher Francis Hutcheson (1694–1746) proposed a 'moral sense theory' — that humans have an innate faculty analogous to the senses that perceives moral qualities directly — influencing Hume's and Adam Smith's accounts of moral psychology.

Mary Astell (1666–1731), sometimes called the 'first English feminist,' argued in 'A Serious Proposal to the Ladies' (1694) for women's education and rational autonomy, and in 'Some Reflections Upon Marriage' (1700) exposed contradictions in political theory that justified male authority over women while opposing arbitrary political power.

The concept of 'natural right' in early modern political philosophy (Hobbes, Locke, Grotius) grounds political authority in individual rights that exist in a hypothetical state of nature prior to government — contrasting with 'natural law' theories that derive rights from objective moral norms or divine command.

Edmund Burke's 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790) is a founding text of philosophical conservatism, arguing that inherited institutions embody accumulated practical wisdom that abstract reason cannot replace — making tradition and gradual reform preferable to revolutionary change.

Alexis de Tocqueville's 'Democracy in America' (1835–40) offered a philosophical analysis of democratic society's virtues and pathologies — including the risk of 'soft despotism' and the 'tyranny of the majority' — that remains one of the most penetrating analyses of liberal democracy.

The philosopher Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) coined 'survival of the fittest' and developed social Darwinism — applying evolutionary theory to society — but his views were roundly critiqued by philosophers including T.H. Huxley, who argued the 'naturalistic fallacy' runs through evolutionary ethics.

The American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) founded both pragmatism and semiotics — the study of signs — arguing that a sign functions through its object (what it stands for) and its interpretant (the effect it has on a mind), a triadic relation that shaped 20th-century linguistics and literary theory.

The German philosopher Ernst Cassirer (1874–1945) developed a 'philosophy of symbolic forms' — arguing that human culture is constituted through symbols (language, myth, art, science) — as an alternative to both reductionist naturalism and idealist metaphysics.

Edmund Husserl's distinction between 'noesis' (the act of consciousness) and 'noema' (the intentional content of that act) — what one intends — is central to phenomenological method and allows a study of the structures of consciousness independent of its psychological or physical substrate.

Simone Weil's concept of 'decreation' describes the spiritual practice of renouncing the illusory self — not suicide, but the relinquishing of one's place in the world to make room for God — drawing on both Platonic and Hindu spiritual sources to develop a distinctive philosophy of self-transcendence.

The concept of 'ideology' in Marx's philosophy refers to the system of beliefs and values that serves the interests of the dominant class by disguising or justifying exploitation — including religion, law, and liberal political theory as forms of 'false consciousness.'

Ernst Bloch's 'The Principle of Hope' (1954–59) developed a Marxist philosophy of the 'not-yet' — arguing that utopian desire, expressed in dreams, art, and social movements, is a real ontological drive toward unfulfilled human possibilities that should be the core of critical philosophy.

The concept of 'negative dialectics,' developed by Theodor Adorno in his 1966 work of the same name, argues that dialectical reason must remain critical and resist the impulse toward a final synthesis or identity — every conceptual totality does violence to the particular things it subsumes.

The philosopher Herbert Marcuse's 'One-Dimensional Man' (1964) argued that advanced industrial society neutralizes radical opposition by absorbing it into consumer culture, creating a 'one-dimensional' consciousness unable to imagine alternatives to the existing order.

The philosophy of 'recognition' — that self-consciousness and human dignity require acknowledgment by others — was developed by Hegel in the 'Phenomenology of Spirit' and revived by Axel Honneth and Charles Taylor, influencing theories of multiculturalism and identity politics.

The concept of 'communicative rationality' in Habermas distinguishes between strategic action (using others as means to one's ends) and genuinely communicative action (oriented toward mutual understanding and agreement) — grounding a normative theory of discourse and democracy in the pragmatics of language.

The political philosopher Philip Pettit developed 'republicanism' as a third alternative to liberalism and communitarianism, arguing that freedom is best understood as non-domination — freedom from the arbitrary power of others — rather than non-interference (Berlin's negative liberty).

Arne Næss (1912–2009), founder of deep ecology, drew on Spinoza and Gandhi to argue that human and non-human beings have equal intrinsic value, that current human interference with nature is excessive, and that fundamental changes in basic economic, technological, and ideological structures are needed.

The ecofeminist philosopher Val Plumwood argued in 'Feminism and the Mastery of Nature' (1993) that the domination of nature and the domination of women share the same conceptual framework — the logic of colonization — and that ecological crisis requires a feminist philosophical critique.

The philosopher Mark Johnson and George Lakoff's 'embodied cognition' thesis in 'Philosophy in the Flesh' (1999) argued that abstract thought is built from bodily metaphors — we understand argument as war, time as a resource, the mind as a container — undermining the Cartesian view of reason as disembodied.

The philosopher Thomas Nagel's 'The View from Nowhere' (1986) argued that objective scientific description and subjective first-person experience are both real and irreducible, and that neither can fully account for the other — positing a 'fragmentation of the world picture' at the heart of modern thought.

The philosopher Robert Nozick's 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974) argued that any state more extensive than a minimal 'night-watchman state' violates individual rights — presenting a libertarian alternative to Rawls and arguing that the free market is just if it arises from just transactions.

The concept of 'overlapping consensus' in Rawls's 'Political Liberalism' (1993) holds that a liberal society can achieve stability without requiring all citizens to share the same comprehensive doctrine — they can agree on political principles for different reasons derived from their different moral, religious, or philosophical views.

Will Kymlicka's 'Multicultural Citizenship' (1995) developed a liberal theory of minority rights, arguing that cultural membership is a precondition for autonomous choice and that liberals must therefore support special rights for national minorities and ethnic groups within liberal states.

The 'capability approach' originated with Amartya Sen in his critique of welfarism and resource-based theories of justice, arguing that what matters morally is not resources or welfare but the real opportunities — capabilities — people have to lead lives they have reason to value.

The debate between 'ideal' and 'non-ideal' political theory (Charles Mills, Amartya Sen) asks whether philosophy should focus on perfectly just societies as a benchmark or on identifying the most urgent injustices and feasible improvements in existing unjust conditions.

Philippa Foot's 'Natural Goodness' (2001) revived neo-Aristotelian naturalism in ethics, arguing that human goodness — virtue — is a form of natural goodness evaluated by the standards appropriate to humans as a kind of natural being, just as a wolf's goodness consists in having good teeth and hunting well.

The concept of 'moral encroachment' (Rima Basu, Georgi Gardiner) argues that high-stakes practical and social considerations can affect what it is epistemically appropriate to believe about persons — that believing someone is a criminal when the evidence is thin may be epistemically wrong as well as morally wrong.

The philosophy of 'well-being' (or welfare) identifies three main theories: hedonism (well-being consists in pleasure and absence of pain), desire satisfaction (well-being consists in getting what one wants), and objective list theories (well-being consists in achievement of certain objective goods regardless of desire).

The concept of 'grounding' in metaphysics — the relation by which some facts hold in virtue of other, more fundamental facts — has become a central concept in recent analytic metaphysics, with Kit Fine and Gideon Rosen developing it as a formal relation distinct from causation, supervenience, and logical entailment.

The philosopher L.A. Paul's 'transformative experience' (2014) argues that some major life experiences — like having a child or joining a religion — are 'epistemically transformative' (you cannot know what they are like until you have them) and 'personally transformative' (they change who you are), creating unique decision-theoretic puzzles.

The field of 'moral psychology' studies empirically how people actually make moral judgments and decisions, using psychological research; findings about in-group favoritism, disgust responses, and implicit bias challenge idealized models of moral reasoning in traditional ethics.

The ancient Indian philosophical debate on 'inference' (anumana) developed remarkably detailed theories; Dignaga's wheel of reasons (trairupya) identifies three conditions for a valid inference — the reason must be present in the subject, co-present with the property being inferred, and absent from all counter-examples.

The Daoist philosopher Liezi (c. 400 BCE), whose eponymous text contains some of the most creative philosophical fiction in Chinese tradition, explored themes of transformation, relativity of perspective, and the dissolution of the boundary between self and world.

The Neo-Confucian concept of 'gewu' (investigation of things) — from the 'Great Learning' — prompted centuries of debate: Wang Yangming interpreted it as rectifying one's own mind, while Zhu Xi interpreted it as the empirical investigation of the principle (li) immanent in things.

The Zen philosopher Dogen Zenji (1200–1253 CE) argued in 'Shobogenzo' that 'to study the self is to forget the self' — the practice of zazen is not a means to enlightenment but is itself enlightenment, collapsing the means-ends distinction fundamental to goal-directed thinking.

The Yoruba philosophical concept of 'ori' — the personal spiritual intuition or destiny — is a form of individual essence that, unlike the Western soul, is chosen before birth and continuously cultivated through moral action, constituting a distinctly African account of personal identity and agency.

The Akan concept of 'sunsum' (spirit or soul) and 'kra' (the life force from God) constitute distinct aspects of the Akan person, with sunsum being the source of character and personality while kra is the divine element — a distinctly African dualism different from Cartesian mind-body division.

Latin American philosophy of 'liberation' (filosofía de la liberación), developed by Enrique Dussel and others in the 1970s, critiques European philosophy as a product of colonial domination and argues for a philosophy beginning from the perspective of the excluded, the poor, and the colonized.

The Nahua (Aztec) concept of 'nepantla' — a state of being in between, of transition and ambiguity — was recovered by Chicana philosopher Gloria Anzaldúa as a philosophical metaphor for the borderland experience of those inhabiting multiple, conflicting cultural identities.

The Lakota concept of 'mitákuye oyásʼiŋ' (all my relations) expresses a philosophical worldview in which all beings — human, animal, plant, mineral, and spiritual — are understood as relatives in a web of relationships, providing an Indigenous ethical basis for environmental responsibility.

The Māori concept of 'mana' refers to authority, prestige, and power derived from one's relationship to the divine and the community — not merely personal achievement — and has been analyzed by philosophers as an example of a relational and non-individualistic account of personhood and social standing.

The Confucian philosopher Dong Zhongshu (179–104 BCE) correlated Heaven, Earth, and humanity through a philosophy of 'resonance' (ganying) — arguing that human virtues align with cosmic forces and that the ruler's moral conduct directly affects natural phenomena like floods and droughts.

The Korean philosopher Yi Hwang (Toegye, 1501–1570) and Yi I (Yulgok, 1536–1584) debated the Four-Seven Thesis — how principle (li) and material force (qi) relate to the Four Beginnings (compassion, shame, modesty, right and wrong) and Seven Emotions — one of the most refined metaphysical debates in East Asian philosophy.

The Japanese philosopher Watsuji Tetsuro (1889–1960) developed 'fudoki' (climate and culture theory) arguing that human existence is inherently 'climatic' — shaped by specific geographic and seasonal environments — providing an alternative to Heidegger's abstract Dasein.

The philosopher Nel Noddings developed 'relational ethics of care' as an educational philosophy, arguing that the caring relation — not abstract principles — should be the foundation of moral education, and that good schools model the care of an idealized parent.

The concept of 'epistemic justice,' extended from Fricker to collective contexts, asks how social structures can distribute epistemic power fairly — who gets to be a knower, whose knowledge counts, and who has the power to set the terms of epistemic evaluation.

The contemporary 'new materialism' (Rosi Braidotti, Karen Barad, Jane Bennett) challenges both representationalism and anthropocentrism, arguing that matter itself is lively, agentic, and entangled — drawing on quantum physics, feminist theory, and Spinozistic philosophy.

Object-Oriented Ontology (OOO), developed by Graham Harman from Heidegger's tool-analysis, argues that objects have a hidden, 'withdrawn' reality that exceeds their relations and effects — providing an anti-correlational metaphysics that places objects rather than human access at the center.

The philosopher Quentin Meillassoux's 'speculative materialism' in 'After Finitude' (2008) attacks 'correlationism' — the post-Kantian view that we only have access to the correlation between thought and world — arguing for a 'great outdoors': contingent reality that is absolutely independent of thought.

The concept of 'slow philosophy' or 'philosophical practice' — philosophy as a living, transformative practice rather than academic exercise — was revived by Pierre Hadot's studies of ancient philosophy as 'spiritual exercises' and is practiced in philosophical counseling and café-philosophy movements.

The philosopher Byung-Chul Han's 'The Burnout Society' (2010) offers a philosophical diagnosis of contemporary achievement culture — arguing that performance imperatives create a 'positivity excess' that produces depression, ADHD, and burnout, more oppressive than traditional disciplinary societies.

The concept of 'philosophical counseling' — applying philosophical dialogue to personal and existential problems rather than psychological therapy — was developed by Gerd Achenbach in Germany in 1981 and is practiced globally as an application of philosophical practice to everyday life.

The concept of 'epistemic cowardice' — giving deliberately vague or uncommitted answers to avoid controversy or displeasure — has been identified by philosophers including Jennifer Saul as a genuine intellectual vice that undermines honest discourse and democratic deliberation.

The concept of 'luck egalitarianism' in distributive justice (G.A. Cohen, Eric Rakowski) holds that inequalities are unjust only when they arise from bad brute luck (circumstances beyond one's control), not from option luck (deliberate gambling) — a position criticized by Elizabeth Anderson for failing to respect persons.

Annette Baier's 'Moral Prejudices' (1994) argued that Hume, not Kant, is the correct model for moral philosophy — emphasizing trust, emotion, and the 'second-order trust' (trust in our trust relations) as foundational to morality, over Kantian autonomy and rational law.

The philosopher Stanley Cavell's 'The Claim of Reason' (1979) connected Wittgenstein's ordinary language philosophy with moral philosophy, arguing that moral conflict is often about refusing to acknowledge others' humanity — making ethics a matter of acknowledgment and voice rather than mere principle.

The 'Cambridge change' — named after debates among Cambridge philosophers — is a merely relational change: when you grow taller than your neighbor, your neighbor undergoes a Cambridge change (from 'taller than you' to 'shorter than you') without any intrinsic change in themselves, raising questions about what changes really matter.

The philosopher Susanne Langer's 'Philosophy in a New Key' (1942) argued that art is a form of 'non-discursive symbolism' expressing the dynamic felt quality of human experience — providing a philosophy of art that explains artistic meaning without reducing it to propositional content.

The concept of 'aesthetic experience' — a distinctive form of absorbed, interested attention to a work's formal properties and meaning — has been central to aesthetics since Kant; Monroe Beardsley and George Dickie debated whether it is a real psychological category or a myth of aesthetic theory.

The concept of 'moral imagination,' analyzed by Mark Johnson and Iris Murdoch, refers to the capacity to perceive a moral situation with sensitivity, to envision alternative courses of action, and to empathize with those affected — a capacity that rules and principles alone cannot provide.

The philosophical study of 'silence' — developed by philosophers including Max Picard and Gemma Corradi Fiumara — explores silence not as mere absence of sound but as a distinct mode of communication, presence, and understanding, relevant to philosophy of language and contemplative traditions.

The philosopher Alvin Goldman developed 'reliabilism' — a form of externalist epistemology holding that a belief is justified if it is produced by a reliable cognitive process — providing a naturalistic account of epistemic justification grounded in psychology and cognitive science.

The 'lottery paradox' (Henry Kyburg, 1961) shows that apparently reasonable epistemic principles lead to contradiction: if you have a fair lottery of one million tickets, you are justified in believing of each ticket that it will lose, yet you know some ticket will win — so you both do and do not know someone will win.

The concept of 'epistemic akrasia' — believing something against one's own better epistemic judgment — is controversial: some philosophers deny it is possible (you believe what you take to be most reasonable), while others argue it occurs when unconscious biases override conscious assessments.

The concept of 'dogmatism' in epistemology refers to accepting a proposition without adequate evidence or despite counter-evidence; in Pyrrhonism it means holding any positive belief about non-evident matters — making any confident assertion an intellectual vice.

The concept of 'epistemic closure' — if you know P and you know P entails Q, do you know Q? — is contested in epistemology; Dretske and Nozick deny closure, arguing that knowledge-tracking conditions can fail to transmit across known entailments in radical skeptical scenarios.
