Contextualism in epistemology holds that 'knows' is a context-sensitive term — what counts as knowledge varies with the conversational context and the standards being applied — explaining how we can truly say both 'I know I have hands' and 'I don't know I'm not a brain in a vat.'

Timothy Williamson's 'Knowledge and Its Limits' (2000) argued that knowledge is the most fundamental factive mental state — not analyzable into belief plus truth plus justification — and that the margin for error principle explains most epistemic puzzles including the sorites and the KK principle.

The naturalized epistemology program, launched by Quine's 1969 essay 'Epistemology Naturalized,' argues that epistemology should be replaced by or continuous with empirical cognitive science — abandoning the project of giving an a priori account of knowledge and justification.

The philosophy of science concept of 'underdetermination' holds that any body of evidence is logically compatible with multiple mutually incompatible theories — undermining the idea that science converges on a single true description of the world and motivating scientific anti-realism.

Scientific realism holds that mature scientific theories are approximately true and that the unobservable entities they posit (electrons, quarks) really exist; Bas van Fraassen's 'constructive empiricism' counters that we should only accept theories as empirically adequate — true of observable phenomena.

The 'no-miracles argument' for scientific realism (Hilary Putnam) holds that the predictive success of mature science would be a miracle unless its theories were approximately true; the 'pessimistic meta-induction' (Laudan) counters that past successful theories were later abandoned, so current ones probably are false too.

The concept of 'laws of nature' in philosophy of science divides into regularity theories (laws are mere regularities — Hume, Ramsey-Lewis), necessitarian theories (laws involve real natural necessity — Armstrong), and dispositionalist theories (laws reflect real causal powers in things).

The 'circularity problem' in evolutionary epistemology — using cognition to justify the reliability of cognition — illustrates why naturalizing epistemology is philosophically difficult: we cannot step outside our cognitive faculties to evaluate them from a neutral perspective.

The contemporary debate on 'extended cognition' has spawned related debates on 'scaffolded minds' and 'cognitive offloading' — asking to what extent genuinely cognitive processes can be distributed across organisms, environments, and other agents, and what this means for responsibility and personhood.

The philosopher Ned Block distinguished access consciousness (information being available for use in reasoning, reporting, and guiding action) from phenomenal consciousness (the subjective feel of experience) — a distinction that has structured two decades of debate in philosophy of mind.

Global workspace theory (Bernard Baars) proposes that consciousness arises when information is broadcast widely through a 'global workspace' in the brain — a cognitive architecture that makes information available to many specialized processes, distinguishing conscious from unconscious processing.

Predictive processing theory (Andy Clark, Karl Friston) proposes that the brain is a prediction machine — constantly generating and updating probabilistic predictions about sensory input — suggesting that perception, action, and cognition are unified in a single computational framework.

The concept of 'mental causation' asks how mental events cause physical events — how my desire for coffee causes my hand to reach for the cup — and is made problematic by the 'exclusion argument': if physical events have sufficient physical causes, mental causes appear to be redundant.

The philosophy of color in the context of cognitive science reveals that our color categories are not universal — the Pirahã language of the Amazon lacks basic color terms, and languages divide the color spectrum differently — raising questions about whether colors are objective properties or cognitive-cultural constructs.

The concept of 'panpsychism' — the view that consciousness or mind-like properties are fundamental and ubiquitous in nature — has been revived by philosophers including Philip Goff as a response to the hard problem of consciousness, arguing that if physics is causally complete, consciousness must be part of the physical world at its most basic level.

The philosophical problem of 'combination' in panpsychism — how micro-level proto-conscious properties in individual particles combine to form unified human consciousness — is known as the 'combination problem' and is considered by many to be as serious as the hard problem of consciousness itself.

Illusionism about consciousness (Keith Frankish) holds that phenomenal consciousness is itself an illusion — we are deceived by our own introspective reports about the nature of our experience — dissolving rather than solving the hard problem by denying there is any special 'what it is like.'

The philosopher Jesse Prinz's 'embodied appraisal theory of emotion' combines James-Lange bodily response theory with cognitive appraisal theory, arguing that emotions are perceptions of bodily states that represent core relational themes (danger, loss, injustice) relevant to the organism.

The concept of 'affordances' (James Gibson, 1979) describes the action possibilities that environments offer to organisms — a chair affords sitting, a rock affords throwing — influencing philosophy of perception (anti-representationalism) and human-computer interaction design.

The debate on 'mental representation' divides those who think the mind works by manipulating inner symbolic representations (Fodor's language of thought) from those who argue cognition is better understood through dynamical systems theory, embodied action, and direct environmental coupling (van Gelder, Thompson).

The philosophy of 'emergence' distinguishes weak emergence (higher-level patterns not predictable in practice from lower-level properties, but in principle reducible) from strong emergence (genuinely novel causal powers that cannot in principle be reduced), with consciousness being the canonical alleged example of the latter.

The concept of 'type identity theory' (Smart, Place) holds that mental state types are identical with neural state types — pain just is C-fiber firing — while 'token identity theory' (Davidson) holds only that each individual mental event is identical with some physical event, allowing multiple realizability.

The argument from multiple realizability (Putnam, 1967) holds that the same mental state (pain) can be realized in different physical substrates (human brains, octopus neurons, silicon chips), suggesting that mental state types cannot be identical with specific physical types — supporting functionalism over type physicalism.

The concept of 'personal autonomy' — governing oneself in accordance with reasons and values that are genuinely one's own — is central to both Kantian ethics and liberal political philosophy; threats to autonomy include manipulation, addiction, and internalized oppression that shapes preferences without genuine endorsement.

The philosopher Elizabeth Anderson's 'democratic equality' in 'What Is the Point of Equality?' (1999) criticizes luck egalitarianism for being 'obsessed with the metaphysics of luck,' arguing that the real point of equality is to abolish oppression and create a democratic community of equals.

The concept of 'sufficientarianism' in distributive justice holds that what matters is that people have 'enough' — a threshold of resources, capabilities, or welfare — rather than equality per se; Harry Frankfurt argued that what matters morally is whether people have sufficiency, not whether some have more than others.

The philosopher Brian Barry's 'impartialist' theory of justice in 'Justice as Impartiality' (1995) argues that principles of justice must be ones that no one could reasonably reject from behind a veil of ignorance — combining Rawlsian contractarianism with T.M. Scanlon's contractualism.

The concept of 'cosmic pessimism' — associated with philosophers like Philipp Mainländer and Julius Bahnsen who radicalized Schopenhauer — holds that non-existence is preferable to existence, and that the universe itself has a drive toward annihilation rather than continuation.

Anti-natalism, defended by philosopher David Benatar in 'Better Never to Have Been' (2006), argues that coming into existence is always a serious harm — since existence always involves suffering while non-existence involves no deprivation — making procreation morally wrong.

The concept of 'existential risk' (Nick Bostrom, Toby Ord) identifies risks that could permanently curtail humanity's long-term potential — asteroid impacts, engineered pandemics, misaligned AI — arguing these deserve priority concern even at low probabilities given the stakes of what would be lost.

The philosopher Toby Ord's 'longtermism' holds that the most important determinant of our moral priorities is the astronomical scale of the future — if humanity has a long future ahead, the potential value of good outcomes vastly outweighs near-term goods, making far-future welfare morally dominant.

The concept of 'moral uncertainty' — not knowing with confidence which ethical theory is correct — has generated a literature on how to act under such uncertainty; Will MacAskill argues for 'moral parliament' models that weight different theories by credence, while others argue uncertainty supports risk-aversion about serious wrongs.

The philosopher Shelly Kagan's 'The Geometry of Desert' examines how the distribution of welfare among individuals who deserve different amounts affects the goodness of outcomes — a formal study showing that commonly held moral views about desert lead to complex and sometimes counterintuitive prescriptions.

The philosopher Jonathan Dancy developed 'holism in the theory of reasons' — the idea that a consideration that is a reason in one situation may not be a reason, or may be the opposite reason, in a different situation — challenging the universal, principle-based approach to ethics.

The concept of 'semantic minimalism' (Cappelen and Lepore) holds that the literal content of most sentences is context-invariant — only a small class of context-sensitive expressions (indexicals like 'I', 'now', 'here') varies with context — against contextualist and relativist views of meaning.

The debate between 'semantic internalism' and 'semantic externalism' asks whether meaning is determined by internal mental states or by external factors — environment and social context; Putnam and Burge's arguments for externalism showed that meaning is not entirely 'in the head.'

The 'knowledge argument' against physicalism — Frank Jackson's Mary case — prompts the 'phenomenal concepts strategy' as a physicalist response: Mary gains new phenomenal concepts (a new way of representing the same physical facts), not new facts, when she sees red for the first time.

The philosophy of fiction examines the ontological status of fictional entities (Sherlock Holmes does not exist, but claims about him can be true), the logic of fictional names, and the nature of narrative understanding — asking how fiction can impart knowledge about real emotions, moral situations, and human nature.

The concept of 'artistic expression' — how works of art express emotions — divides into expression theories (art expresses the artist's emotions), arousal theories (art evokes emotions in the audience), and Kendall Walton's make-believe theory (artworks prescribe imagining certain emotional responses).

Roger Scruton's aesthetics defended the concept of 'serious' art — art that rewards aesthetic attention by revealing the meaning and humanity in its subject — against avant-garde art that, he argued, is merely provocative without genuine artistic achievement.

The concept of 'formalism' in philosophy of art (Clive Bell, Roger Fry) holds that aesthetic value lies entirely in 'significant form' — the arrangement of lines, colors, and shapes — independent of representational content or emotional expression, reducing all art to abstract composition.

The 'intentional fallacy' (Wimsatt and Beardsley, 1946) holds that the author's intention is irrelevant to the correct interpretation of a work — what matters is the public meaning of the text, not the private psychological states of its creator, a thesis that shaped structuralist and post-structuralist literary theory.

Hans Robert Jauss's 'aesthetics of reception' (Rezeptionsästhetik) argued that a work of art's meaning is not fixed by its creator but is co-constituted through the 'horizon of expectations' that readers bring to it — making interpretation a historically situated dialogue between text and audience.

The philosophy of music asks what music expresses, how it represents, and whether purely 'absolute' music (without program or words) can convey determinate meaning; Eduard Hanslick's formalist claim that music is 'tonally moving forms' was countered by Susanne Langer's symbolism of 'felt life.'

The concept of 'philosophical anthropology' — the systematic philosophical study of human nature — encompasses the question of what distinguishes humans from animals and machines, developed by Helmuth Plessner's theory of 'eccentric positionality' (humans alone have a reflexive distance from their own existence).

The philosopher Arnold Gehlen argued in 'Man: His Nature and Place in the World' (1940) that humans are 'instinct-deficient beings' — lacking the fixed instincts of animals — who compensate through institutions, culture, and technology that provide the stability needed for action.

The concept of 'philosophical zombie' is used not just to argue against physicalism but to support the philosophical analysis of conceivability as evidence for possibility; Daniel Dennett responds that zombies are simply inconceivable once one fully understands what physical processes are like.

The concept of 'narrative self-constitution' (Marya Schechtman) holds that personal identity is constituted by the narrative a person implicitly or explicitly tells about themselves — one is the protagonist of one's own life story — though critics question whether all personal identity requires narrative.

The philosophy of sport's debate about 'technologically enhanced performance' — asking whether doping or genetic enhancement undermines the meaning of sport — draws on the philosophy of human nature, the distinction between 'natural' and 'artificial,' and questions about what sporting achievement is supposed to demonstrate.

The philosopher Peter Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) argued that moral responsibility is grounded in our 'reactive attitudes' — resentment, indignation, gratitude — not metaphysical freedom of the will, and that philosophical arguments for determinism cannot undermine these attitudes from within our practice.

The Grice-Searle debate on the nature of meaning in the 1960s–70s established that speaker's meaning (what the speaker intends to communicate) is distinct from sentence meaning (the semantic content of the sentence) — a distinction central to pragmatics, implicature, and the theory of speech acts.

The philosophy of 'testimony' distinguishes reductionism (Hume: testimony-based belief requires positive reasons for trust) from anti-reductionism (we are prima facie entitled to trust testimony) — with social implications for how institutions should treat eyewitness evidence and expert testimony.

The 'extended epistemology' movement argues that sources of knowledge extend beyond individual minds to include communities, traditions, and institutions — prompting questions about the epistemic responsibilities of groups, the epistemology of memory institutions, and distributed knowledge.

The concept of 'peer disagreement' in epistemology asks: if you and an equally rational, equally informed person disagree about a proposition, should you reduce your confidence to split the difference? The 'conciliationist' view says yes, while the 'steadfast' view says you may maintain your original belief.

The philosopher Michael Dummett argued for 'anti-realism' about meaning — that the meaning of a sentence is given by its verification conditions, not its truth conditions — implying that statements without decidable truth conditions are meaningless, leading to intuitionist logic that rejects the law of excluded middle.

The concept of 'truth aptness' asks which sentences are in the business of being true or false: moral sentences, according to expressivists, are not truth-apt; according to quasi-realists (Blackburn), they can earn their truth aptness through philosophical reconstruction without abandoning the non-cognitivist starting point.

The philosophical concept of 'vagueness' — predicates like 'bald,' 'tall,' and 'heap' that admit of borderline cases — is addressed by degree theories (truth comes in degrees), epistemic theories (borderline cases have definite truth values, we just cannot know them), and supervaluationism (borderline claims have no determinate truth value).

The concept of 'expressivism' in metaethics holds that moral sentences do not describe facts but express non-cognitive attitudes — Ayer's emotivism (moral sentences express emotions), Blackburn's quasi-realism (they express pro-attitudes), and Gibbard's norm-expressivism (they express acceptance of norms).

The concept of 'dispositions' in metaphysics — fragility, solubility, beliefs — raises the question of whether unmanifested dispositions are real: a glass that was never dropped but would have broken if dropped seems to have a real property; philosophers debate whether dispositions are fundamental or reducible to categorical bases.

The debate between 'four-dimensionalism' (perdurance: objects persist by having temporal parts — like movies have frames) and 'three-dimensionalism' (endurance: objects are wholly present at each moment they exist) is central to metaphysics of persistence and has implications for personal identity.

The concept of 'haecceitism' in modal metaphysics holds that there are purely qualitative differences between possible worlds differing only in which individual exists in which role — a view associated with David Kaplan and contrasted with anti-haecceitism (which identifies individuals by their qualitative properties alone).

The philosopher Kit Fine distinguished 'essence' from 'necessity': while it is necessary that Socrates belongs to the singleton {Socrates}, it is not part of Socrates's essence — essence is what something is, not just what is necessarily true of it, opening a new approach to modal metaphysics.

The philosophical concept of 'truthmakers' — what in the world makes a proposition true — has generated contemporary debates about sparse vs. abundant truthmakers, the truthmakers for negative and general truths, and whether truth is always grounded in the concrete world or can float free of it.

The concept of 'ontological commitment' (Quine) holds that a theory commits us to whatever objects must exist for the theory's statements to be true — 'to be is to be the value of a bound variable' — providing a method for determining what a theory's ontology requires.

The concept of 'physicalism' (or materialism) holds that everything that exists is physical; arguments for it include the causal closure of physics (physical events have sufficient physical causes) and the success of physical explanation; arguments against include phenomenal consciousness and normativity.

Jonathan Edwards (1703–1758), America's greatest colonial philosopher, synthesized Calvinist theology with Lockean empiricism and Newtonian science, arguing that beauty — the harmony and proportion of all things in God's being — is the fundamental nature of reality.

Josiah Royce (1855–1916), American idealist philosopher, developed the concept of 'loyalty to loyalty' as the foundation of ethics — a person should be loyal to their community's causes in a way that also supports the loyalty of others, binding individuals to the wider human community.

George Santayana's 'Scepticism and Animal Faith' (1923) argued that ordinary animal faith — practical trust in the external world — underlies all knowledge, and that skepticism refuted by scepticism itself: the sceptic must act in the world, implicitly trusting what they claim to doubt.

The concept of 'philosophical therapy' in the Wittgensteinian tradition holds that philosophical problems are not deep truths awaiting discovery but confusions arising from linguistic misuse — the therapist's task is to dissolve them by showing how language goes wrong, returning words to their ordinary usage.

The concept of 'defeasibility' in epistemology — a belief can be justified while remaining open to revision in light of new evidence — is central to foundationalism debates; defeasible justification is weaker than deductive justification but stronger than mere opinion.

The 'infinite regress problem' in epistemology — any justified belief B requires a prior justified belief B1, which requires B2, etc., leading to infinite regress — motivates foundationalism (there are basic beliefs requiring no further justification), coherentism (beliefs justify each other holistically), and infinitism (the infinite chain is acceptable).

The philosopher Ernest Sosa distinguishes 'animal knowledge' (reliably produced true belief without reflective awareness) from 'reflective knowledge' (knowing that one knows — achieved through reflective understanding of why one's belief is reliable), proposing that the latter is a higher epistemic achievement.

The concept of 'phenomenal intentionality' holds that the intentionality — aboutness — of mental states is grounded in phenomenal consciousness rather than in functional or causal relations, providing a response to externalist accounts of mental content.

The philosopher Daniel Stoljar argues that physicalism is not yet falsified by consciousness because we are ignorant of physical nature — the 'ignorance hypothesis' holds that we simply don't know enough about physical reality to know whether it can explain consciousness.

The concept of 'neurophenomenology' (Francisco Varela) attempts to bridge phenomenology and cognitive neuroscience by using first-person phenomenological methods to constrain and inform third-person neuroscientific investigation of consciousness.

The concept of 'collective intentionality' — the capacity for groups to have shared intentions, beliefs, and desires — is philosophically controversial; Searle holds it is irreducible to individual intentionality, while Michael Bratman and others seek to analyze it through individual intentions and interdependence.

The concept of 'implicit bias' refers to automatic, unconscious attitudes or stereotypes that influence judgment and action; its philosophical significance lies in questions about moral responsibility, epistemic rationality, and what counts as an agent's 'own' attitudes when they are unconscious and disavowed.

The philosopher Miranda Fricker's analysis of 'hermeneutical injustice' explains why victims of sexual harassment historically lacked the conceptual vocabulary to understand or articulate their experience — a form of epistemic injustice arising from systematic gaps in collective hermeneutical resources.

The concept of 'moral deference' — relying on others' moral judgments rather than forming your own — raises a puzzle: epistemically rational but perhaps morally inappropriate, as if the content of a moral judgment is that it must be made for oneself rather than outsourced.

The concept of 'standpoint epistemology' holds that social position shapes epistemic access — oppressed groups may have privileged epistemic standpoints on oppression because they experience it directly; this is not mere 'experience,' but a structured social position enabling certain insights unavailable from dominant positions.

The philosophy of medicine asks whether medicine is a science (like physics), an applied science (like engineering), or a craft (like cooking); the concept of 'disease' is particularly contested — whether it refers to a value-neutral biological dysfunction or necessarily involves judgments of badness relative to human interests.

The concept of 'moral bootstrapping' — whether we can derive moral authority for foundational institutions (constitutions, first legislatures) that do not yet have legitimate authority — is a puzzle for social contract theory explored by philosophers including Jeremy Waldron.

The concept of 'moral psychology' in neo-Aristotelian ethics examines how virtues and character traits function as stable dispositions that are manifest across situations — challenged by 'situationist' social psychology research suggesting people's behavior is more situation-dependent than character-based.

The concept of 'pragmatic encroachment' holds that practical stakes can affect what it is rational to believe — if the stakes of being wrong are high, you need more evidence to count as 'knowing'; this links epistemology and practical rationality in a way that pure epistemology traditionally resisted.

The philosopher Michael Walzer's 'Spheres of Justice' (1983) argued that justice requires complex equality — different goods (money, political power, medical care, education) should be distributed according to the principles appropriate to each sphere, preventing dominant goods from colonizing other spheres.

The philosopher G.A. Cohen's critique of Rawls argued that the difference principle — inequalities justified if they benefit the least advantaged — is undermined when the talented demand higher wages to work harder; Cohen argued this reflects a failure of 'ethos,' not just unjust institutions.

Christine Korsgaard's 'Sources of Normativity' (1996) argues that moral obligations originate in our own practical identities — the norms we must endorse to constitute ourselves as agents — providing a Kantian account of normativity without Kant's appeal to pure practical reason.

The concept of 'constructivism' in metaethics (Korsgaard, Street, Rawls) holds that moral truths are constructed through procedures of rational deliberation or reflective endorsement — neither discovered as mind-independent facts nor merely expressed as non-cognitive attitudes.

Sharon Street's 'Darwinian dilemma' argues that evolutionary debunking applies equally to moral realism and error theory: if our moral attitudes were shaped by evolution, either moral realism requires a massive coincidence between evolutionary pressures and moral facts, or moral attitudes are not tracking independent moral facts.

The concept of 'moral progress' raises questions about its direction and driver — is it driven by expanding circles of moral concern (Singer), improving moral epistemology (Railton), changes in material conditions (Marx), or the democratic spread of power to previously excluded groups (Dewey)?

The concept of 'dirty hands' in political philosophy (Walzer after Sartre) describes the dilemma of the political leader who must do wrong to do right — for example, ordering torture to prevent a terrorist attack — and must bear moral guilt for the necessary transgression.

The just war tradition — tracing from Cicero, Augustine, and Aquinas through Grotius and Vitoria to modern international law — identifies conditions for when war is justified (jus ad bellum) and how it must be conducted (jus in bello), with contemporary debates including the ethics of drone warfare and targeted killing.

The philosopher Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency' doctrine holds that when a political community faces threats to its very existence, it may violate ordinary just war constraints — including targeting civilians — as a last resort, raising profound questions about the limits of moral rules.

The concept of 'reparations' in political philosophy — compensating historically wronged groups for past injustices — raises philosophical questions about collective responsibility, group membership, benefit and burden transfer across generations, and the currency of reparation.

The concept of 'transitional justice' examines how societies emerging from authoritarian regimes or civil conflicts can deal with past human rights abuses through truth commissions, tribunals, amnesties, and reparations — balancing accountability, reconciliation, and social reconstruction.

The concept of 'democratic deliberation' in political philosophy (Habermas, Rawls, Gutmann and Thompson) holds that legitimate democratic decisions must emerge from public reasoning among citizens who exchange justifications — not merely from aggregating preferences through voting.

Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951) demonstrates that no voting system satisfying a small number of reasonable conditions (unanimity, independence of irrelevant alternatives, non-dictatorship) can consistently aggregate individual preference orderings into a social ordering — a fundamental result in social choice theory with implications for democratic theory.

The concept of 'constitutional patriotism' (Dolf Sternberger, Jürgen Habermas) holds that national identity and loyalty should be grounded in shared commitment to universal constitutional principles rather than ethnic or cultural particularity — a proposed basis for post-nationalist civic identity.

The 'capabilities approach' in international development ethics holds that development should be measured not by GDP but by what people are actually able to do and be; Nussbaum's list includes life, health, bodily integrity, senses/imagination/thought, emotions, practical reason, affiliation, play, and control over one's environment.

The philosophical debate on 'global justice' asks whether principles of distributive justice apply globally — between nations as well as within them — with cosmopolitan theorists (Pogge, Beitz) arguing yes, and statists (Walzer, Miller, Nagel) arguing that special obligations apply only to co-citizens of a shared political community.

The concept of 'intergenerational justice' asks what obligations current generations have to future ones — particularly regarding climate change, resource depletion, and institutional design — with Rawls, Parfit, and Edward Page offering competing accounts of what fairness requires across time.

The philosopher Henry Shue's 'Basic Rights' (1980) argued that all human rights presuppose 'subsistence rights' (the right to minimum economic security) as preconditions for the exercise of any other rights, challenging the traditional priority of civil and political rights over economic and social rights.

The 'positive-negative rights' distinction holds that negative rights (right to not be interfered with) impose only duties of forbearance, while positive rights (rights to food, health, education) impose duties of provision — a distinction criticized as overly simplistic since all rights require positive institutional enforcement.

The concept of 'recognition' in contemporary political theory — following Hegel's master-slave dialectic and Taylor's 'politics of recognition' — holds that individuals and groups need acknowledgment of their dignity and particular identity to form a positive self-relation; denial of recognition is a form of oppression.

The philosopher Onora O'Neill's Kantian approach to global justice argues that the basic obligations of justice are requirements of non-deception and non-coercion — duties owed to all persons as rational agents — grounding a demanding account of international justice without appealing to shared institutional membership.

The concept of 'toleration' in political philosophy — permitting what one disapproves of or finds wrong — has a paradoxical structure: one tolerates only what one judges to be wrong or bad, so perfect tolerance ('anything goes') collapses into mere indifference rather than genuine tolerance.

The philosopher Joseph Raz's 'liberal perfectionism' holds that the state may promote valuable ways of living and discourage worthless ones — in tension with neutralist liberalism — arguing that autonomy (the capacity to choose well among valuable options) is the core liberal value, not mere preference satisfaction.

The concept of 'paternalism' in political philosophy — restricting a person's liberty for their own good — divides 'hard paternalism' (overriding autonomous choices) from 'soft paternalism' (overriding only non-autonomous choices); John Stuart Mill's 'harm principle' is standardly read as an absolute prohibition on hard paternalism.

Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler's 'libertarian paternalism' or 'nudge theory' holds that choice architecture can steer people toward better choices without restricting freedom — default enrollment in pension plans, for instance — as a philosophically defensible alternative to both laissez-faire and hard regulation.

The concept of 'algorithmic ethics' examines the moral implications of automated decision-making systems — in hiring, credit scoring, criminal justice — asking about accountability, transparency, discrimination, and whether algorithms can be 'fair' in any morally meaningful sense.

The philosopher Floridi's 'information ethics' holds that all informational objects — not just sentient beings — have intrinsic ontological value and that ethics should be grounded in respect for the informational environment, the 'infosphere,' as a whole.

The concept of 'digital dualism' (Nathan Jurgenson) refers to the false dichotomy between 'online' and 'offline' life — physical and digital are not separate worlds but interpenetrate; the philosophical challenge is to theorize an 'augmented reality' in which digital and physical are co-constitutive.

The concept of 'surveillance capitalism' (Shoshana Zuboff) describes the extractive logic of data-driven platforms — human experience is claimed as raw material, processed into behavioral data products sold to advertisers and institutional buyers — raising philosophical questions about autonomy, consent, and the future of democracy.

The concept of 'transhumanism' holds that humans can and should use technology — genetic engineering, neural interfaces, artificial intelligence — to transcend current biological limitations; its philosophical critics argue this threatens human dignity, authentic experience, and social equality.

Michael Sandel's critique of 'market reasoning' in 'What Money Can't Buy' (2012) argues that extending market logic to domains like education, health, civic life, and friendship corrupts them by crowding out non-market norms like equality, solidarity, and intrinsic value.

The concept of 'objectification' (Martha Nussbaum, Rae Langton) describes treating a person as a mere object — denying their subjectivity, instrumentalizing them, treating them as interchangeable or fungible — a form of disrespect with roots in Kant's categorical imperative.

The concept of 'thick autonomy' holds that genuine autonomy requires not just non-interference (negative autonomy) but substantive conditions — education, material security, social recognition — for the development of the rational and reflective capacities that make choices truly one's own.

The philosopher Michael Bratman's 'planning theory of agency' holds that human agency is distinctive in being guided by temporally extended plans — intentions that persist, coordinate, and constrain future action — providing a framework for akrasia, self-governance, and shared cooperative activity.

The concept of 'intentional action' — a long-standing puzzle in philosophy of action — is addressed by Donald Davidson's account (actions are events caused by beliefs and desires in the right way) and Anscombe's Wittgensteinian account (intentional action is action done for a reason, known without observation).

The concept of 'omission' in moral philosophy asks whether failing to act is morally equivalent to acting — is letting someone drown as bad as pushing them in? Most philosophers hold that there is a morally significant difference between acts and omissions, though consequentialists typically deny this.

The concept of 'moral residue' in cases of moral dilemma distinguishes a 'remainder' — a genuine moral loss that demands acknowledgment — from tragic choice, where we correctly choose the lesser evil; Bernard Williams argued that a person who feels no residue of wrongdoing is morally shallow.

The philosopher Samuel Scheffler's 'Equality and Tradition' (2010) argues against egalitarianism that would require erasing valuable traditions and practices simply because they embody non-egalitarian arrangements, defending a pluralism of values that includes but goes beyond equality.

The concept of 'moral integrity' (Williams) refers to the connection between a person's projects and commitments and their actions — an agent of integrity acts from their deepest commitments rather than performing abstract calculations; Williams argued that utilitarianism threatens personal integrity by requiring agents to calculate impartially.

The concept of 'supererogation' refers to actions that go beyond what duty requires — heroic sacrifice, extraordinary generosity — that are morally praiseworthy but not obligatory; debates about their existence distinguish deontological from consequentialist ethics, since pure consequentialism recognizes no upper limit on moral obligation.

The philosopher Onora O'Neill's 'Constructions of Reason' (1989) argued that Kant's ethics is fundamentally about principled reasoning that can be shared with others — not a mysterious inner faculty of pure practical reason — making it a more accessible and practical moral philosophy.

The concept of 'normative ethics' contrasts with metaethics (which asks what ethics is) and applied ethics (which applies principles to cases); normative ethics itself divides into consequentialism (outcomes), deontology (duties and rights), and virtue ethics (character) as the three main theoretical frameworks.

W.D. Ross's theory of 'prima facie duties' in 'The Right and the Good' (1930) holds that there are multiple basic moral duties — promise-keeping, non-maleficence, beneficence, fidelity, gratitude, reparation, self-improvement, and justice — that can conflict, requiring judgment to determine which is most stringent in context.

The 'repugnant conclusion' problem in population ethics led Parfit to develop 'critical level utilitarianism' as a potential solution — adding a person to the world is good only if their welfare exceeds a positive critical level — though this generates its own counterintuitive results.

The concept of 'contractualism' (T.M. Scanlon) holds that morality is fundamentally about what principles we could not reasonably reject when assessing what we owe each other — an approach to ethics grounding obligations in idealized hypothetical agreement without the veil of ignorance.

The debate between 'monism' and 'pluralism' in value theory asks whether all values are ultimately reducible to a single value (goodness, welfare, preference satisfaction) or whether there are genuinely incommensurable values — like knowledge and friendship — that cannot be traded off on a single scale.

Isaiah Berlin's 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958) introduced the negative/positive liberty distinction and argued that value pluralism — the reality of irreconcilable, conflicting ultimate values — means there is no perfect political arrangement, and trade-offs between liberty, equality, and security are unavoidable.

The concept of 'philosophical luck' in the study of philosophical methodology — noting that many philosophical positions are influenced by the cultural and historical context of their proponents — raises questions about whether philosophy makes genuine progress or merely reflects the prejudices of its times.

The concept of 'moral status' — who or what deserves moral consideration and protection — has been challenged by advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience; traditional criteria (rationality, sentience, being a subject of a life) are tested by entities like sophisticated AI systems and minimally conscious patients.

The concept of 'ecological grief' or 'solastalgia' (Glenn Albrecht) — the distress caused by environmental change and loss of one's home environment — has generated philosophical reflection on new forms of existential suffering tied to climate change and the human relationship to place.

The philosopher Robin Wall Kimmerer's 'Braiding Sweetgrass' (2013) articulates an Indigenous botanical philosophy of reciprocity, gratitude, and mutual flourishing between humans and other species — expressing an animist ontology that challenges Western nature-culture binaries.

The concept of 'speciesism' (Peter Singer) — treating individuals less favorably on the basis of their species membership — is analogous to racism and sexism, and is criticized by animal rights philosophers as an unjustifiable form of discrimination that should be overcome by expanding our moral circle.

The Kantian philosopher Christine Korsgaard's 'Fellow Creatures' (2018) argues that the Kantian practical identity framework extends to animals — they too value their lives from their own perspective — providing a Kantian foundation for animal rights without reducing ethics to sentience.

The concept of 'relational autonomy' in feminist philosophy holds that autonomy is not a property of isolated individuals but develops and is sustained through relationships — certain social conditions (non-oppressive norms, supportive relations) are necessary for genuine self-governance.

The philosopher Frantz Fanon's 'Black Skin, White Masks' (1952) applied phenomenological analysis to the racialized body — the 'epidermal schema' — arguing that racism disrupts the lived experience of Black people by imposing a white gaze that alienates them from their bodies and selves.

The philosopher Lewis Gordon develops 'Africana existential philosophy' — drawing on Du Bois, Fanon, and Sartre — to explore the existential predicament of people of African descent in a racist world, including the bad faith of choosing 'flight' from one's Blackness rather than affirming it.

Charles W. Mills's 'The Racial Contract' (1997) argued that modern political philosophy's implicit social contract is actually a racial contract — an agreement among whites to benefit from and maintain racial privilege — challenging the race-blindness of liberal political theory from Locke to Rawls.

The concept of 'epistemic oppression' (Dotson) refers to a persistent and unwarranted diminishment of a person's epistemic agency — their capacity to generate, transmit, or receive knowledge — as a structural feature of oppressive social systems rather than individual acts of prejudice.

The concept of 'willful ignorance' in social philosophy refers to the active maintenance of ignorance about privileged social positions and their relation to oppression — Charles Mills's 'epistemology of ignorance' argues that white ignorance is not passive but is actively produced and maintained.

The concept of 'decolonization of knowledge' argues that Western academic philosophy has systematically excluded and devalued non-Western philosophical traditions — African, Asian, Indigenous, Latin American — and calls for restructuring curricula and epistemic practices to reflect global philosophical diversity.

The philosopher Nishitani Keiji (1900–1990) of the Kyoto School developed a philosophy of nihility and emptiness — drawing on Zen Buddhism, Nietzsche, and Heidegger — arguing that confronting nihility (the abyss beneath existence) can transform into sunyata (emptiness as openness) through religious awakening.

The philosopher Taitetsu Unno applied Buddhist philosophy to the modern condition, arguing that 'self-awakening' — recognizing one's fundamental impermanence and interconnectedness — offers a non-theistic response to modern alienation more honest than either secularism or theism.

The philosopher Masao Abe argued that Buddhism offers a more adequate account of emptiness (sunyata) than Western concepts of nothingness, and that Buddhist-Christian dialogue requires genuine mutual transformation rather than superficial comparison — developing a distinctive philosophy of inter-religious encounter.

The Indian philosopher Jiddu Krishnamurti (1895–1986) rejected all religious and philosophical authority, arguing that truth cannot be approached through any organization, teacher, or tradition — and that genuine inquiry requires complete psychological freedom from conditioning and belief.

The philosopher Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950) developed 'integral philosophy' — synthesizing Vedanta, evolutionary theory, and his own spiritual experience — arguing that consciousness is evolving from matter through life and mind to supermind, and that human transformation is the next stage of cosmic evolution.

B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), leader of the Dalit liberation movement, developed a philosophical critique of the caste system grounded in Buddhism's radical egalitarianism — converting to Buddhism in 1956 and arguing that Buddhism, properly understood, provides an Indian foundation for democratic rights and human dignity.

The philosopher K.C. Bhattacharyya (1875–1949), one of the most original Indian philosophers in the Western sense, argued that the 'subject as freedom' — the self's capacity for negation and self-transcendence — is irreducible to any objective or naturalistic account, developing a distinctly Indian philosophy of subjectivity.

The concept of 'philosophical poverty' — the exclusion of economically marginalized perspectives from academic philosophy — has been highlighted by philosophers including Charles Mills and Kristie Dotson, arguing that class bias shapes which problems are taken seriously and whose experience is philosophically acknowledged.

The concept of 'disability studies philosophy' challenges the 'medical model' of disability (disability as pathology to be cured) with a 'social model' (disability as social exclusion of people with non-standard bodies), raising questions about normality, access, identity, and the limits of enhancement ethics.

The concept of 'compulsory able-bodiedness' (Robert McRuer) in crip theory holds that normative cultural and social systems systematically privilege able-bodied norms in ways that oppress disabled persons, analogous to how compulsory heterosexuality operates in queer theory.

The concept of 'fatphobia' has been analyzed philosophically as a form of injustice that combines bodily stigma, reduced epistemic credibility, and social exclusion — connecting philosophy of embodiment, feminist philosophy, and theories of structural injustice.

The philosopher T.M. Scanlon's 'Being Realistic About Reasons' (2014) defended normative realism — the view that there are mind-independent normative facts about reasons — while arguing that this metaethical view has no troubling epistemological implications since our access to reasons does not require a mysterious faculty.

The concept of 'buck-passing' in metaethics (Scanlon) holds that 'good' does not name a property but 'passes the buck' to other properties that provide reasons for favorable attitudes — 'X is good' means 'there are reasons to favor X,' avoiding the naturalistic fallacy by grounding value in reasons.

The concept of 'moral testimony' — whether it is appropriate to simply defer to others' moral judgments — has generated debate about whether morality, unlike empirical matters, requires first-person engagement; purely testimonial moral beliefs may be epistemically acceptable yet morally objectionable.

The 'experience machine' and 'utility monster' thought experiments test consequentialism's commitment to maximizing welfare — the utility monster (Nozick) holds all utility, so maximizing utility requires enslaving everyone to it — revealing that pure aggregation violates fundamental intuitions about the separateness of persons.

Rawls's 'difference principle' has been distinguished from 'prioritarianism' (Parfit, Temkin): prioritarianism weights improvements to worse-off people more heavily, but does not require that all inequalities benefit the worst off; Rawls's principle is lexically prior to utility maximization, prioritarianism is not.

The concept of 'negative responsibility' (Williams) refers to consequentialism's implication that one is equally responsible for outcomes one fails to prevent as for those one causes — a counterintuitive extension of moral responsibility that ignores the moral significance of one's own agency and projects.

The philosopher Jerry Fodor's 'modularity of mind' thesis held that the mind consists of encapsulated, domain-specific input systems (visual, auditory, etc.) feeding into a central processor; this architectural claim, disputed by connectionionist models, shapes debates about cognitive architecture and artificial intelligence.

The philosopher Ruth Millikan's teleological theory of meaning holds that representations have content in virtue of their biological function — what they were selected to represent — providing a naturalistic account of intentionality that grounds mental content in evolutionary history.

The concept of 'inference to the best explanation' (Gilbert Harman, Peter Lipton) holds that we are justified in accepting the hypothesis that best explains our evidence — an abductive form of reasoning central to scientific practice but philosophically contested as potentially circular.

The concept of 'epistemic virtue' — character traits of excellent epistemic agents like open-mindedness, intellectual courage, and thoroughness — has been developed by philosophers including James Montmarquet, John Greco, and Linda Zagzebski, connecting virtue ethics to epistemology.

The concept of 'epistemic trust' — trusting others as sources of knowledge — is irreducible to belief in testimony: it involves a relationship of reliance, respect, and appropriate expectation of reciprocal disclosure, analyzed by Annette Baier as a three-place relation between truster, trusted, and matters entrusted.

The concept of 'rational belief revision' (Isaac Levi, Hansson) examines how agents should update their beliefs when receiving new information — including how to contract (remove beliefs) as well as expand (add beliefs), governed by coherence and informational economy constraints.

The concept of 'disjunctivism' in the philosophy of perception holds that perception and hallucination are fundamentally different kinds of mental state — not different species of the same genus — so that genuine perception is constituted by direct acquaintance with external facts, not an inner mental representation.

John McDowell's 'Mind and World' (1994) argued that there is a 'frictionless' coherentism in both Quine and Davidson that fails to account for how experience can genuinely constrain belief — his solution is to 'naturalize' Aristotle, seeing conceptual capacities as part of second nature acquired through upbringing.

The concept of 'epistemic paternalism' asks when it is permissible to restrict or guide someone's epistemic activities for their own epistemic good — including questions about informed consent, epistemic nudges, and whether algorithmic filtering is a form of epistemic paternalism.

The philosopher Bas van Fraassen's 'empirical stance' requires not only a commitment to empirical adequacy but a stance — an attitude, a set of values, virtues, and commitments — rather than a theory, as a philosophical response to the question of what it is to be an empiricist.

The concept of 'semantic holism' holds that the meaning of individual terms and sentences cannot be determined in isolation but only in relation to the entire system of a language or theory — a view associated with Quine, Davidson, and the Wittgenstein of the 'Philosophical Investigations.'

The philosophy of science concept of 'explanation' divides into deductive-nomological models (Hempel: explanations are deductive arguments citing laws), causal-mechanical models (Salmon: explanations trace causal processes), and unificationist models (Friedman, Kitcher: explanations reduce the number of patterns needed to account for the world).

The concept of 'mechanism' in philosophy of science and biology refers to organized entities and activities whose temporal and spatial organization produces regular changes — Machamer, Darden, and Craver's 'new mechanism' provides a framework for explanation in biology and neuroscience that transcends the law-based Hempelian model.

The concept of 'reduction' in philosophy of science asks when one theory or science can be reduced to another — when chemistry reduces to physics, or psychology to neuroscience; Ernest Nagel's formal account requires bridge laws connecting theoretical vocabularies, while anti-reductionists deny such laws exist for special sciences.

The concept of 'scientific models' — physical, mathematical, or conceptual representations used in scientific practice — raises philosophical questions about how models relate to theories, how they represent the world, and whether idealized models that are strictly false can still explain.

The concept of 'ceteris paribus laws' ('other things being equal') in the special sciences — laws that hold in the absence of interfering factors — raises questions about whether such laws are genuinely lawlike or merely vacuous; Jerry Fodor defended them as irreducible features of the special sciences.

The philosopher Helen Longino developed a 'contextual empiricism' arguing that scientific knowledge is inherently social and values-laden — background assumptions, funding structures, and social norms inevitably shape scientific inquiry — requiring public scrutiny and uptake of criticism to achieve objectivity.

The concept of 'scientific consensus' raises philosophical questions about when disagreement among scientists should discount consensus — in climate science, vaccine safety, evolutionary biology — and how experts should communicate uncertainty without undermining public understanding.

The philosopher Philip Kitcher's 'Science, Truth, and Democracy' (2001) argued for 'well-ordered science' — science whose agenda is shaped by democratic processes reflecting the full range of citizens' values — challenging the idea that science is autonomous from social and political accountability.

The concept of 'truth pluralism' holds that there are different properties that play the truth role in different domains — correspondence in empirical claims, coherence in mathematics, superassertibility in ethics — providing a unified but domain-sensitive account of truth (Crispin Wright, Michael Lynch).

The concept of 'deflationism about truth' (Horwich's minimalism, disquotationalism) holds that 'it is true that P' says nothing more than P itself — 'truth' is not a substantive property requiring philosophical explanation, but a logical device for generalization and endorsement.

The correspondence theory of truth holds that a proposition is true if and only if it corresponds to the facts; challenges include specifying what 'correspondence' is and what 'facts' are — Wittgenstein's Tractatus gave a precise version, and Davidson argued the concept of correspondence does more harm than good.

The coherence theory of truth holds that a belief is true if it coheres with an overall system of beliefs — associated with idealist philosophers like Bradley and Blanshard; its critics argue that a coherent system of beliefs could be systematically false if disconnected from reality.

The pragmatist theory of truth (Peirce, James, Dewey) holds that truth is what inquiry converges on in the long run (Peirce), what works in practice (James), or what resolves problematic situations (Dewey) — each version is contested for blurring the distinction between truth and utility.

The concept of 'epistemic situatedness' in feminist philosophy holds that all knowledge claims are made from a particular social location — there is no 'view from nowhere' — and that acknowledging this situatedness is necessary for honest and politically responsible inquiry.

Donna Haraway's 'A Cyborg Manifesto' (1985) proposed the cyborg as a philosophical figure transcending dualisms (human/machine, nature/culture, male/female) and as a model for feminist theory that embraces partial identities, contradictions, and ironic political mythologies.

The concept of 'postgenderism' holds that advances in biotechnology and cognitive science may eventually allow humans to transcend gender — eliminating biological sex differences through reproductive technology and genetic modification — raising philosophical questions about whether gender is an essential or contingent feature of human identity.

The concept of 'cisnormativity' in queer theory refers to the cultural assumption that cisgender identity is the natural, neutral default while transgender identities require special explanation — a form of structural bias analyzed using tools from philosophy of language (presupposition) and social ontology.

The philosopher Charles Mills's 'Black Rights/White Wrongs' (2017) extends his racial contract framework to critique mainstream political philosophy for its silence on white supremacy, arguing that ideal political theory built on abstraction from racial reality is an obstacle to understanding and rectifying injustice.

The concept of 'white ignorance' (Mills) describes the systematically produced and maintained ignorance about the workings of racial oppression — not mere individual ignorance but a cognitive orientation that serves the interests of white supremacy by rendering its mechanisms invisible.

The philosopher María Lugones developed 'world-travelling' as a feminist philosophical method — the capacity to understand another person's world from within, including their sense of humor and ease — as a basis for solidarity across difference and an alternative to assimilation.

The philosopher Joy James developed 'captive maternal' theory to analyze the philosophical and political significance of Black women's caregiving labor under conditions of captivity and racial capitalism, extending Fanon's analysis to the domestic sphere.

The concept of 'ableism' — the system of beliefs and practices that devalues disabled bodies and minds relative to norms of able-bodiedness — has been analyzed philosophically as both a form of oppression and an epistemic orientation that shapes what counts as competence, rationality, and flourishing.

The philosopher Patricia Hill Collins's 'Black Feminist Thought' (1990) argued that Black women occupy a distinctive 'outsider within' standpoint — inside institutions that exclude them — generating a distinctive epistemological standpoint and a tradition of philosophical reflection on interlocking oppressions.

Gottlob Frege's distinction between 'sense' (Sinn) and 'reference' (Bedeutung), introduced in his 1892 essay 'Über Sinn und Bedeutung,' showed that two expressions can refer to the same object yet differ in cognitive significance — 'the morning star' and 'the evening star' both refer to Venus but convey different modes of presentation.

Saul Kripke's 'Naming and Necessity' (1980) argued that proper names are 'rigid designators' that refer to the same individual in every possible world, challenging descriptivist theories and establishing that identity statements like 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' are necessarily true though known only a posteriori.

The causal theory of reference, developed by Kripke and Hilary Putnam in the 1970s, holds that the reference of a name is fixed by an initial 'baptism' and then passed through causal-historical chains of use, rather than by descriptive content associated with the term in speakers' minds.

Hilary Putnam's 'twin earth' thought experiment argued that 'meanings just ain't in the head': two speakers on Earth and Twin Earth may have identical mental states yet their words 'water' refer to different substances (H₂O vs. XYZ), showing that semantic content depends on external environment.

Al-Ghazali's 'The Incoherence of the Philosophers' (Tahāfut al-Falāsifa, 1095 CE) launched a systematic critique of Aristotelian philosophy in the Islamic world, arguing that doctrines such as the eternity of the world, God's lack of knowledge of particulars, and the denial of bodily resurrection were philosophically untenable and religiously dangerous.

Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198 CE) responded to Al-Ghazali in 'The Incoherence of the Incoherence' (Tahāfut al-Tahāfut), defending Aristotelian philosophy and arguing that reason and religious revelation are ultimately compatible — his commentaries on Aristotle profoundly shaped both Islamic and European scholastic thought.

Ibn Tufayl's philosophical novel 'Hayy ibn Yaqzan' (12th century CE) described a child raised in isolation on a deserted island who independently discovers philosophical and spiritual truths through reason alone, illustrating the power of natural human intellect to attain knowledge without revelation or social instruction.

Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037 CE) developed the 'flying man' thought experiment — a person created floating in void, deprived of all sensory input — to argue that such a person would still be aware of their own existence, anticipating Descartes's cogito and establishing the soul's independence from bodily sensation.

Modal logic, formalized by C.I. Lewis in the early 20th century and extended by Saul Kripke with possible-worlds semantics in the 1960s, provides a rigorous framework for reasoning about necessity, possibility, and counterfactuals by quantifying over accessible possible worlds in formal models.

Deontic logic, pioneered by G.H. von Wright in 1951, applies modal operators to normative concepts of obligation, permission, and prohibition, enabling formal analysis of ethical and legal reasoning — though it faces paradoxes like the 'Good Samaritan' and 'contrary-to-duty' problems that challenge simple systems.

Temporal logic, developed by Arthur Prior in the 1950s–60s, introduces operators for 'it will be the case that' and 'it was the case that,' enabling formal reasoning about time-indexed truths and playing a crucial role in computer science for specifying and verifying concurrent systems.

Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) invented the literary essay as a philosophical genre — the word 'essai' meaning 'attempt' or 'trial' — using personal anecdote and skeptical self-examination to explore the instability of human judgment, the diversity of customs, and the limits of self-knowledge.

Spinoza's political philosophy, articulated in the 'Tractatus Theologico-Politicus' (1670) and 'Tractatus Politicus' (1677), argued that democracy is the most rational form of government, that freedom of thought is inalienable, and that the purpose of the state is to secure individual freedom rather than impose religious or ideological conformity.

David Hume's moral philosophy, developed in 'A Treatise of Human Nature' (1739–40) and 'An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals' (1751), grounded ethics in sentiment rather than reason, arguing that moral judgments express emotional responses — approval and disapproval — rather than reporting objective facts.

Aristotle's concept of 'phronesis' (practical wisdom) — the intellectual virtue that enables one to deliberate correctly about human goods and act well in particular circumstances — was distinguished from theoretical wisdom (sophia) and technical knowledge (techne), forming the cornerstone of his virtue ethics.

The Epicurean school, founded by Epicurus (341–270 BCE), held that the highest good is ataraxia (tranquility of mind) and aponia (freedom from bodily pain), achievable through moderate pleasures, friendship, philosophical reflection, and withdrawal from politics — not hedonistic indulgence, as commonly misunderstood.

The Skeptical Academy, led by Arcesilaus and later Carneades in the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE, argued against the Stoic doctrine of kataleptic impressions (infallible perceptions) by claiming that for any impression that seems certain, an equally convincing contrary impression can be constructed, supporting suspension of judgment (epochē) on all matters.

Plotinus (205–270 CE), founder of Neoplatonism, described reality as emanating in hierarchical levels from 'the One' — the absolutely simple, ineffable first principle — through Nous (intellect) to Soul and finally the material world, with philosophy's goal being the soul's return to union with the One through contemplation.

Religious experience as a source of knowledge of God's existence was defended by William Alston in 'Perceiving God' (1991), arguing that mystical perception — like sense perception — can be epistemically basic, providing justification for belief in God that does not depend on prior argument.

The problem of religious diversity — that mutually incompatible religious traditions each claim truth and salvific insight — was analyzed by John Hick as evidence for a 'pluralist hypothesis': all major religions are culturally conditioned responses to a single transcendent Real, none having exclusive access to ultimate truth.

Mysticism across traditions — from Christian apophatic theology (Meister Eckhart), to Sufi fana (annihilation of self in God), to Buddhist nirvana — has been analyzed philosophically by W.T. Stace as involving a common 'extrovertive' or 'introvertive' core of unity experience that transcends cultural differences.

The bioethics debate over end-of-life care was transformed by the distinction between killing and letting die — active euthanasia versus withdrawal of treatment — challenged by James Rachels in 1975, who argued there is no intrinsic moral difference between the two when the intention and outcome are the same.

The ethics of organ donation raises the 'dead donor rule' — vital organs should only be taken from dead patients — which is complicated by debates over whole-brain versus higher-brain criteria for death, and whether patients in a permanent vegetative state should count as dead for transplant purposes.

The philosopher Peter Singer's 'Animal Liberation' (1975) applied the principle of equal consideration of interests — suffering matters equally regardless of species — to argue that factory farming and animal experimentation constitute 'speciesism,' an unjustifiable form of discrimination analogous to racism and sexism.

Genetic ethics explores philosophical questions raised by CRISPR and germline editing, including whether 'designer babies' violate children's right to an open future (Joel Feinberg), whether genetic enhancement is compatible with human dignity, and whether traits selected by parents constitute authentic expressions of their future child's identity.

The philosophy of economics examines the foundations of economic reasoning, including the debate over whether rational choice theory describes actual human behavior or only idealized agents, and whether economic models should be judged by predictive accuracy (Friedman) or by the realism of their assumptions (methodological realism).

The concept of 'adaptive preferences' — desires shaped by unjust circumstances that lead people to want less than they deserve — was analyzed by Jon Elster and Amartya Sen as a key limitation on preference-satisfaction theories of well-being, since people can be conditioned to prefer their own oppression.

The philosophical analysis of tragedy, from Aristotle's account of catharsis (the purgation or clarification of pity and fear through dramatic representation) to Nietzsche's claim in 'The Birth of Tragedy' that Greek tragedy affirms life through the interplay of Apollonian form and Dionysian chaos, remains central to aesthetics.

The paradox of fiction — why we feel genuine emotions like pity, fear, and admiration toward characters and events we know to be fictional — was analyzed by Kendall Walton through his 'make-believe' theory, arguing that fictional emotions are quasi-emotions generated within games of pretence rather than genuine beliefs about reality.

Narrative theory in philosophy, developed by Paul Ricoeur in 'Time and Narrative' (1984–88), argued that human time is fundamentally narrative time — we understand our lives and history through the configuration of events into stories — making narrative identity constitutive of selfhood rather than merely descriptive of it.

The Pyrrhonian skeptic Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE) catalogued ten 'modes' (tropoi) of suspension of judgment — including the variability of perception across different animals, persons, circumstances, and conditions — arguing that for any claim, equally strong contrary evidence exists, warranting epochē (suspension) rather than dogmatic assertion.

The Stoics developed the doctrine of 'oikeiôsis' (appropriation or affiliation), arguing that all rational beings have a natural affinity first for themselves, then for others in concentric circles of concern — a theory that grounds both natural law and cosmopolitanism in the rational structure of human psychology.

Marcus Aurelius's 'Meditations' (2nd century CE), a private philosophical journal in Stoic tradition, advocated living according to reason and nature, accepting what lies outside one's control, and treating all persons as fellow rational beings worthy of benevolence — a practical ethics of inner freedom amid external constraint.

The early modern controversy between 'occasionalism' (Nicolas Malebranche) — which denied any real causal power to created things, attributing all causation to God's direct activity — and the Leibnizian doctrine of 'pre-established harmony' — which attributed genuine causation to monads but explained coordination through God's initial design — reflects deep tensions in early modern metaphysics.

The philosophy of AI consciousness asks whether artificial systems could ever be genuine moral patients deserving ethical consideration — a question that depends on contested theories of consciousness and what constitutes morally relevant sentience, making it one of the most practically urgent issues in contemporary philosophy of mind.

Digital ethics investigates the moral dimensions of digital technologies: algorithmic bias and discrimination, data privacy and surveillance, the ethics of social media platforms as epistemic and political environments, and the responsibilities of technology designers toward affected communities.

Climate philosophy examines the unique ethical challenges of anthropogenic climate change — including collective action problems, intergenerational justice, the special obligations of wealthy nations toward vulnerable populations, and whether climate disruption constitutes a 'perfect moral storm' that systematically defeats normal ethical reasoning.

The non-identity problem, posed by Derek Parfit in 'Reasons and Persons' (1984), challenges future-oriented ethics: if our policies determine who will be born, and future persons who result from harmful policies would not exist under better policies, it seems we cannot have harmed them — yet intuitively we should still choose better policies.

Epistemic injustice in testimony — 'testimonial injustice,' analyzed by Miranda Fricker in 'Epistemic Injustice' (2007) — occurs when a hearer gives a speaker reduced credibility due to identity prejudice (race, gender, class), wronging the speaker in their capacity as a knower and distorting collective knowledge.

Hermeneutical injustice, the second form of epistemic injustice identified by Miranda Fricker, occurs when a gap in collective interpretive resources places someone at an unfair disadvantage when trying to make sense of their own social experiences — as when the lack of concepts like 'sexual harassment' left victims unable to articulate what was wrong with their situation.

The philosophical analysis of humor by Kant distinguished the comic from the beautiful: laughter arises from the 'sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing' — a cognitive release when an anticipated resolution collapses — anticipating incongruity theories that remain central to contemporary philosophy of humor.

The philosophy of sport examines what constitutes athletic achievement, the ethics of performance-enhancing drugs, whether sport has intrinsic value, and the significance of rule-following — with thinkers like William Morgan arguing that sport is a practice with internal goods that can be corrupted by treating it purely as a means to external rewards.

The Confucian concept of 'ren' (仁, benevolence or humaneness) — cultivated through ritual practice, self-cultivation, and loving relationships — was articulated by Confucius as the supreme virtue from which all others flow, achievable through lifelong moral effort and expressed in treating others with consideration and reciprocity.

Mencius (372–289 BCE), the most important Confucian after Confucius himself, argued for the innate goodness of human nature, identifying four moral sprouts — compassion, shame, modesty, and moral discrimination — as natural tendencies requiring cultivation to become full virtues, against the view of Xunzi that human nature is bad.

Xunzi (c. 310–235 BCE) argued against Mencius that human nature is bad (xing e 性惡) and that moral goodness is an achievement of ritual and education, not a natural endowment — anticipating later Western debates between Hobbes (natural selfishness) and Rousseau (natural goodness) by more than a millennium.

Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE), founder of Mohism, challenged Confucian ritual ethics with a utilitarian-style principle of 'jian ai' (impartial caring): all persons deserve equal concern regardless of their relationship to us, and moral judgments should be evaluated by whether they increase benefit and decrease harm for all.

The School of Names (Ming jia) in Classical Chinese philosophy, represented by thinkers like Gongsun Long and Hui Shi, engaged in paradoxical investigations of language and reality — Hui Shi's 'ten paradoxes' explored infinity, similarity, and change, while Gongsun Long's 'white horse' paradox argued a white horse is not a horse, probing the relationship between universals and particulars.

The Legalist (fajia) philosopher Han Fei (c. 280–233 BCE) argued for rule by impersonal law and institutional design rather than by virtuous rulers, anticipating modern political science: a good state needs clear laws, reliable enforcement, and incentive structures that harness self-interest, not moral suasion or personal loyalty.

The Mahayana Buddhist philosophical school of Yogācāra (4th–5th century CE), associated with Vasubandhu, argued for 'vijñaptimātratā' (consciousness-only or idealism): what we take to be an external world is actually a projection of consciousness, with no mind-independent objects existing outside the stream of conscious experience.

The Madhyamaka school of Buddhist philosophy, founded by Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE), argued for the 'emptiness' (śūnyatā) of all phenomena — including emptiness itself — meaning that nothing has intrinsic, independent existence but arises in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual imputation.

The philosophy of punishment debates whether its justification is backward-looking (retributivism: punishment is deserved for wrongdoing) or forward-looking (consequentialism: punishment deters, rehabilitates, or incapacitates), with mixed theories attempting to capture both — and abolitionist views challenging whether state punishment is ever justified.

H.L.A. Hart's 'The Concept of Law' (1961) distinguished 'primary rules' (obligations on citizens) from 'secondary rules' (rules about rules — recognition, change, and adjudication), arguing that a legal system is a union of these two types and that the 'rule of recognition' determines what counts as valid law in a given society.

Ronald Dworkin challenged legal positivism in 'Taking Rights Seriously' (1977) by arguing that law consists not only of rules but also of principles — standards with weight that must be balanced — and that judges are bound by these principles even in hard cases, where they cannot simply exercise 'discretion.'

The philosophy of mathematics encompasses foundational debates between logicism (Frege, Russell: mathematics reduces to logic), formalism (Hilbert: mathematics is a formal game with symbols), and intuitionism (Brouwer: mathematical objects are mental constructions, and proof must be constructive) — debates made urgent by Gödel's incompleteness results.

Imre Lakatos's 'methodology of scientific research programmes' (1978) proposed that scientific rationality operates at the level of programmes — comprising a 'hard core' of protected assumptions and a 'protective belt' of auxiliary hypotheses — with progress assessed by whether programmes are 'progressive' (generating novel predictions) or 'degenerative.'

Paul Feyerabend's 'epistemological anarchism,' articulated in 'Against Method' (1975), argued that no single scientific method underlies all scientific progress — 'anything goes' — and that science has advanced through violations of accepted method, making methodological pluralism and even non-scientific perspectives epistemically valuable.

The semantic theory of truth, developed by Alfred Tarski in the 1930s, provides a formal definition of truth for formalized languages: 'Snow is white' is true if and only if snow is white — capturing the intuition that truth is a correspondence between sentences and facts while avoiding the liar paradox through a metalanguage/object language distinction.

The concept of 'supervenience' — that mental properties supervene on physical properties, meaning there can be no mental difference without a physical difference — was introduced into philosophy of mind by Donald Davidson and further developed by Jaegwon Kim as a key constraint on any non-reductive physicalism.

Jaegwon Kim's 'causal exclusion argument' challenged non-reductive physicalism: if mental events are distinct from physical events but supervene on them, then when a physical event is causally sufficient for an effect, the mental event is causally excluded — suggesting that mental causation requires either reduction or elimination of the mental.

The philosophical problem of perception — how we come to know external objects through experience — has been debated between 'direct realism' (we perceive mind-independent objects directly), 'representationalism' (we perceive mental representations of objects), and 'disjunctivism' (veridical and hallucinatory experiences are fundamentally different in kind).

Edmund Husserl's phenomenological concept of 'intentionality' — that consciousness is always consciousness-of-something, directed toward objects — and his method of 'epochē' (bracketing the natural attitude to investigate pure experience) laid the foundation for phenomenology as a rigorous philosophical discipline.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of embodiment, developed in 'Phenomenology of Perception' (1945), argued that we perceive the world through a 'lived body' — a pre-reflective bodily schema that shapes all experience — challenging Cartesian dualism and intellectualist theories that reduce perception to cognition.
